title: Warm-up: 1 + 1 = 2
plain: A test problem for checking the submission pipeline. Prove that 1 + 1 = 2.
math: Prove $1+1=2$ in $\mathbb{N}$.

title: Is the complete-pivoting growth factor exactly 8 for 8x8 matrices?
credit: A. Edelman & J. Urschel 2023, arXiv:2303.04892 (also Cryer 1968, Gould 1991 for the g_n <= n history)
premise_risks: Exact values g_n are cited as known only for n ≤ 6 (g_5 = 4.1325, g_6 = 5); check against Edelman–Urschel 2023 before relying on them.
plain: The worst-case complete-pivoting growth is known exactly only for n ≤ 6 (values 1, 2, 2.25, 4, 4.1325, 5). The value g_8 = 8, attained by Hadamard matrices, is conjectured but unproven, and Hadamard matrices are known not to be optimal at n = 12 and 16. Determine g_7 and decide whether g_8 = 8.
math: With $g_n$ as above (real matrices, complete pivoting), prove or disprove $g_8=8$, and determine $g_7$ (known lower bounds from Edelman–Urschel Table 1).

title: Minimal degree of a Jacobian counterexample
credit: Jacobian conjecture (Keller 1939); degree 2: Wang 1980; 2026 counterexamples: arXiv:2608.00222, arXiv:2609.17795, arXiv:2607.22198, arXiv:2607.18186 (Alpöge, van den Essen et al.)
premise_risks: arXiv:2608.00222, arXiv:2609.17795, arXiv:2607.22198, arXiv:2607.18186 (2026 preprints, unrefereed; one has an Isabelle AFP formalization): existence of non-injective Keller maps of C^3 of degree 7, i.e. the upper bound d_3 <= 7 and the claim that the Jacobian conjecture fails in dimension 3. Claim (cubic case) does not logically depend on them.
plain: The 2026 counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture in three variables have degree 7 at best (Alpöge's map has component degrees 7,6,4). Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. Find the smallest degree a three-variable counterexample can have: some number from 3 to 7.
math: Call F ∈ C[x,y,z]^3 a Keller map if det JF ∈ C^×, and let deg F = max_i deg F_i. Prove or disprove: every Keller map F : C^3 → C^3 with deg F <= 3 is injective (equivalently, by Białynicki-Birula-Rosenlicht and the Keller condition, a polynomial automorphism); i.e. d_3 >= 4. (Known: 3 <= d_3 <= 7, where d_3 is the least degree of a non-injective Keller map of C^3.)

title: Singularities of the permanental hypersurface
premise_risks: arXiv:2603.15579 (2026 preprint) is listed in refs and may be the source of the current Sing-codimension bounds (6 <= r <= 2n) quoted in M; these are not used by Claim.
plain: The hypersurface where the n x n determinant vanishes has rational singularities, the mildest kind that matters for much of its geometry. Decide whether the hypersurface where the n x n permanent vanishes has rational singularities for every n, and compute its minimal exponent, a finer measure of how mild a singularity is.
math: Let $X_n=\{\operatorname{per}_n=0\}\subset\mathbb A^{n^2}_{\mathbb C}$ and let $\tilde\alpha(X_n)$ be Saito's minimal exponent (the smallest root of $b_{\operatorname{per}_n}(-s)/(1-s)$), so that $\operatorname{lct}(\mathbb A^{n^2},X_n)=\min\{1,\tilde\alpha(X_n)\}$ and $X_n$ has rational singularities iff $\tilde\alpha(X_n)>1$. For $n=2$, $X_2$ is a nondegenerate quadric cone in $\mathbb A^4$ and $\tilde\alpha=2$. For $\det_n$ the Bernstein--Sato polynomial is $\prod_{i=1}^n(s+i)$, so $\tilde\alpha(\{\det_n=0\})=2$ for all $n$. Determine $\tilde\alpha(X_n)$ for all $n\ge3$ (in particular for $n=3$), and decide whether $X_n$ has rational singularities for every $n$. Note: restricting to a generic linear subspace of dimension $r=\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{Sing}(X_n)$ gives an isolated homogeneous singularity, so $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\ge r/n$. Since $6\le r\le 2n$ is known and $r=2n$ is conjectured, that conjecture would give $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\ge2$ and rational singularities. Sharpened question: is $\tilde\alpha(X_n)=2$ for all $n$, or does $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\to\infty$?

title: Smallest degree of a Keller counterexample in dimension 3
premise_risks: Alpöge counterexample (2026 preprints in refs, e.g. arXiv:2608.00222; formally checked in Isabelle AFP 'Jacobian_Counterexample'): gives d_3 <= 7, i.e. that d_3 is finite. The Claim (d_3 <= 5) does not depend on it.
Other 2026 preprints (2609.17795, 2607.20210, 2607.22198, 2610.24889, 2607.21572, 2609.33491): further counterexamples of degree >= 7 in dim 3 and low-degree ones in dims 4-12; background.
plain: In 2026 the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in three variables. The first explicit counterexample (Alpöge's map) has polynomial degree 7. Wang's theorem says degree 2 is impossible. What is the smallest degree a counterexample in three variables can have? In particular, is there one of degree 3, 4 or 5?
math: Let $d_3$ be the least $d$ such that some polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\max_i\deg F_i=d$ and $\det DF\in\mathbb C^\times$ is not an automorphism. Wang's theorem gives $d_3\ge3$, and Alpöge's map gives $d_3\le7$. Determine $d_3$. In particular, decide whether $d_3\le5$.

title: Smallest dimension of a cubic-homogeneous Jacobian counterexample
credit: Classical HJC(n,3) program: Bass–Connell–Wright (1982), Yagzhev; Hubbers (n ≤ 4 classification); de Bondt–van den Essen arXiv:1609.09753; upper bound de Bondt arXiv:2610.24889.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.24889 (de Bondt, Oct 2026, unrefereed, partly AI-written): source of N₃ ≤ 18 via HJC(18,3); only the upper bound depends on it.
arXiv:2608.00222 / arXiv:2609.17795 (2026 preprints, Alpöge's map and follow-up): the premise that the Jacobian conjecture is false at all; the formal Claim (dimension 5) does not depend on it.
plain: The Jacobian conjecture is now known to fail. A classical reduction says that if it fails at all, it fails for maps of the special form x + (cubic homogeneous terms), but the reduction pays for this by raising the number of variables. Such a cubic counterexample is now known in 18 variables, and none exists in 4 or fewer. What is the smallest number of variables in which one exists?
math: Let $N_3$ be the least $n$ such that there is $H=(H_1,\dots,H_n)$, each $H_i\in\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ homogeneous of degree 3, with $JH$ nilpotent (equivalently, for homogeneous $H$, $\det(I+JH)=1$) and $x+H$ not an automorphism of $\mathbb C^n$. Hubbers' classification of cubic homogeneous nilpotent Jacobians for $n\le4$ gives $N_3\ge5$ ($n=5$ is open as far as we know). De Bondt (arXiv:2610.24889, unrefereed), building on Alp\"oge's map and improving Van Rijn's 19, gives $N_3\le18$. Determine $N_3$; in particular, decide whether the Jacobian conjecture holds for cubic homogeneous maps in dimension 5. Companion: let $d_3$ be the least $\max_i\deg F_i$ over non-invertible Keller maps $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ ($\det JF\in\mathbb C^*$). Wang's theorem gives $d_3\ge3$ and Alp\"oge's map gives $d_3\le7$.

title: Which monodromy groups do Jacobian counterexamples have?
premise_risks: The premise that the Jacobian conjecture was refuted in 2026 rests on 2026 preprints (arXiv:2607.20210, 2607.21572, 2608.00222); if those counterexamples fail, the set M is empty and the question changes completely.
arXiv:2608.02863 (Kistner-Shaska, 2026 preprint): source of S_d, A_d (d = 6, 12, families) as realized monodromy groups.
arXiv:2609.33491 (Fonollosa, 2026 preprint): source of imprimitive wreath-type monodromy groups.
plain: A Keller map (polynomial map with constant nonzero Jacobian) that is not invertible covers a generic point d times, and following the d preimages around loops gives a permutation group, its monodromy. Campbell's 1973 theorem says that if this group is regular (the Galois case), the map is invertible. The 2026 counterexamples realize full symmetric groups and some imprimitive groups. Is Campbell's theorem the only obstruction?
math: For a Keller map $F:\mathbb C^n\to\mathbb C^n$ ($\det JF\in\mathbb C^\times$) of geometric degree $d\ge2$, let $\mathrm{Mon}(F)\le S_d$ be the geometric monodromy group (Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x)/\mathbb C(F)$ acting on the $d$ embeddings). It is transitive, and by Campbell's theorem it is regular only if $d=1$. Let $\mathcal M$ be the set of transitive groups (up to permutation isomorphism) arising as $\mathrm{Mon}(F)$ for non-invertible Keller maps in some dimension; $\mathcal M$ contains $S_d$, $A_d$ (e.g. $d=6,12$ and the families of Kistner-Shaska 2608.02863) and imprimitive wreath-type groups (Fonollosa 2609.33491), and is closed under direct products in product action ($F\times G$). Is $\mathcal M$ exactly the set of non-regular transitive groups? Test case: does some primitive group not containing $A_d$ (e.g. $\mathrm{AGL}(1,p)$ for a prime $p\ge5$, or $\mathrm{PSL}(2,7)$ on 7 points) lie in $\mathcal M$? (A negative answer to the test case means every primitive member of $\mathcal M$ is alternating or symmetric, which would refute the first question.)
lean_gap: Statement left as sorry by design; entire problem depends on 2026 preprints.

title: Charge on a Fermat conductor
plain: Put a unit of electric charge on a perfectly conducting solid x^4+y^4+z^4 <= 1. Show that the surface charge is thinnest exactly at the six flat points (+-1,0,0),... and thickest exactly at the eight points in the diagonal directions.
math: Let $K=\{x^4+y^4+z^4\le1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ and let $\mu=\rho\,d\sigma$ be its Newtonian (capacitary) equilibrium measure, $\sigma$ surface measure on $\partial K$ ($\rho$ is real-analytic and positive since $\partial K$ is analytic). Prove that $\min_{\partial K}\rho$ is attained exactly at $(\pm1,0,0),(0,\pm1,0),(0,0,\pm1)$ and $\max_{\partial K}\rho$ exactly at $3^{-1/4}(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$.

title: Fibonacci-modulated growing Jacobi matrix
credit: Extends Janas-Naboko (periodic modulations, e.g. arXiv:math/0605593) and Swiderski (arXiv:1707.06486) on periodically modulated Jacobi matrices.
plain: Take a Jacobi matrix with zero diagonal and off-diagonal weights sqrt(n). Double the weight at every position where the Fibonacci word has a 1. Periodic modulations of power-growing weights are known to produce spectral phase transitions. Determine the spectral type for this aperiodic modulation.
math: Let $f=f_1f_2f_3\cdots=0100101001001\cdots\in\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ be the Fibonacci word, the fixed point of $0\mapsto01,\ 1\mapsto0$. Let $J$ be the Jacobi operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with $(Ju)_n=a_{n-1}u_{n-1}+a_nu_{n+1}$, where $a_n=\sqrt n\,(1+f_n)$ and $a_0u_0:=0$. Since $\sum 1/a_n=\infty$, $J$ is self-adjoint (Carleman). Determine the spectral type of $J$. In particular: is $\sigma_{ac}(J)\neq\emptyset$? Is $\sigma_{ac}(J)=\mathbb R$? Is the spectrum on some interval pure point or singular continuous?

title: Hearing tetrahedra
credit: Extends Durso (1988, MIT thesis) and Grieser-Maronna, 'Hearing the shape of a triangle' (Notices AMS 2013, arXiv:1208.3163); Kac's question.
results: The heat-invariant count is correct. The polyhedral Dirichlet heat trace gives volume, surface area, the edge sum of L_e times a function of the dihedral angle, and a vertex term (not explicit for general solid angles): 4 numbers against 6 congruence parameters. So the heat trace alone is insufficient.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.28602 (Krejcirik, 2026 survey): used only for the openness check (does not settle the problem); the statement itself assumes nothing from it.
plain: Triangles can be heard: their Dirichlet spectrum determines them up to congruence (Durso 1988; Grieser–Maronna 2013). Show the same for tetrahedra.
math: Let $T_1,T_2\subset\mathbb R^3$ be (nondegenerate) tetrahedra whose Dirichlet Laplacian eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, coincide. Prove that $T_1$ and $T_2$ are congruent.

title: Jacobi matrix of primes
plain: Build an infinite tridiagonal (Jacobi) matrix with zero diagonal and the primes 2, 3, 5, 7, ... on the off-diagonals. The standard criteria for purely absolutely continuous spectrum need the off-diagonal sequence to vary regularly, and they just fail because prime gaps fluctuate. Decide whether the spectrum is nevertheless purely absolutely continuous on the whole real line.
math: Let $J$ be the self-adjoint Jacobi operator on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ given by $(Ju)_n=p_{n-1}u_{n-1}+p_nu_{n+1}$ (with $p_0u_0:=0$), where $p_n$ is the $n$-th prime. It is self-adjoint by Carleman's criterion, since $\sum1/p_n=\infty$. Decide whether $\sigma(J)=\sigma_{ac}(J)=\mathbb R$ with no singular part.

title: Maximal eigenfunction growth beyond surfaces of revolution
credit: C. D. Sogge and S. Zelditch, 'Focal points and sup-norms of eigenfunctions' (arXiv:1311.3999) and its two-dimensional addendum (arXiv:1409.2063, Rev. Mat. Iberoam. 2016).
plain: On the round sphere, some eigenfunctions are as peaked as theory allows, because every geodesic leaving the pole comes back to it. Sogge and Zelditch proved that on any real-analytic surface, maximally peaked eigenfunctions force such a 'pole'. Is rotational symmetry also forced: must such a surface be a surface of revolution?
math: Let $(M,g)$ be a compact boundaryless real-analytic Riemannian surface with $\Delta_g e_j=-\lambda_j^2e_j$, $\|e_j\|_{L^2}=1$. Say $g$ has maximal eigenfunction growth if $\limsup_j \|e_j\|_{L^\infty}/\lambda_j^{1/2}>0$ for some orthonormal eigenbasis. Decide whether every such $(M,g)$ admits a nontrivial isometric $S^1$-action, i.e. is a surface of revolution. (Necessary condition, Sogge-Zelditch 2016: $M$ has a pole $p$, meaning all geodesics from $p$ return smoothly closed at a common time $2T_p$.)
lean_gap: Not formalized: needs real-analytic Riemannian surfaces, the Laplace-Beltrami spectral theory, and isometric circle actions.

title: Non-arithmetic tones of the cube
plain: Many vibration frequencies of a cube's surface come from flat tori and are rational multiples of pi squared. Prove that at least one frequency is not of this form.
math: Let $S$ be the boundary of the unit cube $[0,1]^3$ with its intrinsic flat metric (8 cone points of angle $3\pi/2$), and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $S$. Prove that some eigenvalue of $\Delta$ is not in $\pi^2\mathbb{Q}$.
lean_gap: Not formalized: needs H¹ on a flat cone surface, Dirichlet forms / Friedrichs extension, and spectral theory of the resulting operator; none are in Mathlib.

title: Spikes at the primes
credit: C. R. de Oliveira and G. Q. Pellegrino, '(De)Localization in the Prime Schrodinger Operator', 2001, arXiv:cond-mat/0103313.
plain: Put a bump of fixed height at every prime on the half-line lattice and study the electron (discrete Schrodinger operator). What kind of spectrum does it have inside the free band (-2,2)? If the primes behaved like a random sparse set (Cramer model), the states would be localized (pure point spectrum); is that true for the actual primes?
math: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n)u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with Dirichlet condition $u(0)=0$, $\lambda\ne0$. Determine the spectral type of $H$ on $(-2,2)$. In particular: is the spectral measure restricted to $(-2,2)$ pure point (with exponentially or sub-exponentially decaying eigenfunctions), or does it have a singular continuous part, e.g. near $E=0$?

title: Two-frequency localization
credit: Recognised open problem from the Bourgain-Goldstein / Bourgain-Goldstein-Schlag multi-frequency programme; stated open in arXiv:2603.07180 (2026). Pure point spectrum without exponential decay at fixed Diophantine frequency: Eliasson, Acta Math. 1997.
premise_risks: arXiv:2603.07180 (2026 preprint): the problem relies on its statement that it is unknown whether any fixed Diophantine frequency vector gives localization.
arXiv:2603.10649 (2026 preprint): cited background; content not relied on in the statement.
plain: Take a one-dimensional lattice Schrödinger operator whose potential is the sum of two cosines with frequencies √2 and √3, and make the coupling strong. Prove that for these specific frequencies, not just for almost every frequency pair, almost every phase gives localized eigenfunctions that decay exponentially.
math: For $\lambda>0$ and $\theta\in\mathbb T^2$ let $(H_{\lambda,\theta}\psi)(n)=\psi(n+1)+\psi(n-1)+\lambda\big(\cos2\pi(n\sqrt2+\theta_1)+\cos2\pi(n\sqrt3+\theta_2)\big)\psi(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb Z)$. Prove there is $\lambda_0$ such that for all $\lambda\ge\lambda_0$ and Lebesgue-a.e. $\theta$, $H_{\lambda,\theta}$ has pure point spectrum with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions (Anderson localization).

title: Wind-driven fire confinement threshold
credit: A. Bressan, Differential inclusions and the control of forest fires, J. Differential Equations 2007 (non-isotropic Thm 5)
results: sigma*(a,b) >= Lambda*(a-b), Lambda ~ 1.62621 (isotropic lower bound, arXiv 2610.36919, Thm 4.1). Proof: F contains the disc of radius a-b. Bressan's comparison lemma moves blocking from F to that disc, and rescaling time reduces to unit speed. sigma*(a,b) <= 2 max_{theta in [0,pi]} (a+b cos theta) sin theta (Bressan, Thm 5, non-isotropic case; applies because rho is even and nonincreasing on [0,pi]). This equals 2a at b=0 and tends to (3 sqrt3/2) a as b->a.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.36919 (2026 preprint): isotropic lower bound Lambda ~ 1.6262 (Thm 4.1), used for the lower bound recorded in the notes.
plain: A fire spreads from a point, faster downwind: speed a + b cos(theta) in direction theta (0<=b<a). Firefighters build a barrier at speed sigma. Let sigma*(a,b) be the smallest speed that can confine the fire. Known: 1.626(a-b) <= sigma* <= 2 max (a+b cos theta) sin theta. Improve either bound, especially in the strong-wind limit b/a -> 1, where the lower bound tends to 0 but the upper bound stays near 2.6a.
math: With F_b = conv{r e^{i theta}: 0<=r<=1+b cos theta}, R_0 the open unit disc and Bressan-admissible barriers, prove that for some fixed b in (0,1) the fire can be confined with some sigma < 2 max_theta (1+b cos theta) sin theta, i.e. Bressan's anisotropic upper bound is not sharp.

title: Additive excess for sorting pattern-avoiding sequences
credit: Fredman 1976 (sorting with partial information); Opler, arXiv:2409.07868 (ESA 2025), sorting pattern-avoiding permutations
results: delta_tau >= 0: information-theoretic bound C_tau(n) >= log2|Av_n(tau)| (trivial). delta_tau <= 2: Fredman (1976), any set G of permutations can be sorted with log2|G| + 2n comparisons. Opler (arXiv 2409.07868) gives O((log c_tau +1)n), optimal only up to a constant factor. delta_tau = 0 is known for tau of length 3 in the 132-class (stack sorting, <=2n vs log2 C_n = 2n - O(log n)).
plain: Sorting an array promised to avoid a fixed pattern needs at least log2 of the number of allowed orders comparisons, and Fredman's theorem says 2n more always suffice. How many extra comparisons per element are really needed? Show that fewer than 2n extra suffice for 1324-avoiding inputs, or show that a linear excess is necessary for some pattern.
math: For a permutation τ let C_τ(n) be the minimum worst-case number of comparisons of a decision tree (knowing τ) that sorts a_1,…,a_n under the promise that their order pattern lies in Av_n(τ), and δ_τ = limsup_n (C_τ(n) − log_2|Av_n(τ)|)/n ∈ [0,2]. Prove or disprove: δ_τ = 0 for every permutation τ.

title: Blank jigsaw with few edge shapes
credit: Mossel & Ross (shotgun assembly); Bordenave, Feige, Mossel 2016, arXiv:1605.03086; Nenadov, Pfister, Steger 2017, arXiv:1701.04813
plain: A jigsaw with no picture can only be solved from the shapes of its pieces. Each internal edge is one of k shapes (a tab that fits only its own matching blank), and pieces may be turned. How small can k be if some n×n blank jigsaw still goes together in exactly one way? Counting shows k must be at least about √n, and random puzzles need about n.
math: An $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types is a map assigning to each internal edge of the $n\times n$ grid a type in $[k]$ and an orientation (which side carries the tab); border edges are flat. Its pieces are the $n^2$ unit squares, each regarded as a distinct physical object carrying its four (type, tab/blank) labels up to rotation. An assembly is a placement of all pieces bijectively on the cells, each rotated by a multiple of $90^\circ$, so that every internal edge joins a tab and a blank of the same type and all flat edges lie on the border. Let $k(n)$ be the least $k$ for which some $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types has exactly one assembly up to the four rotations of the whole square. Determine the order of $k(n)$; in particular, is $k(n)=\Theta(\sqrt n)$?

title: Breaking the log k barrier for 3-petal sunflowers
credit: Erdős-Rado 1960 (sunflower conjecture); log k barrier discussed in Alweiss-Lovett-Wu-Zhang, Annals 2021, and Rao, The story of sunflowers, JLMS 2026 (arXiv:2509.14790)
plain: Show every family of more than (o(log k))^k sets of size k (e.g. (log k)^{(1-c)k} or (log log k)^{O(k)}) contains a sunflower with 3 petals.
math: Let f(k,3) be the least m such that every family of m distinct k-element sets contains a 3-petal sunflower. Known: f(k,3) <= (C log k)^k (ALWZ, Rao, Bell-Chueluecha-Warnke). Prove f(k,3) <= (eps(k) log k)^k for some eps(k)->0, e.g. f(k,3) <= (log k)^{(1-c)k} for a constant c>0.
refs: Alweiss, Lovett, Wu, Zhang, Improved bounds for the sunflower lemma, Annals of Math 2021
Bell, Chueluecha, Warnke, Note on sunflowers, Discrete Math 2021
Rao, The story of sunflowers, JLMS 2026 / arXiv:2509.14790
Lovett, PCMI lecture notes: from sunflowers to thresholds

title: Codes avoiding square distances
results: Small values A(1..7)=1,2,4,5,10,12,14 re-verified by exact max-clique. Frankl-Rodl rate<1 argument is correct. The claim that codes with all distances between consecutive squares are polynomial is only correct for windows at linear distance. Constant-weight codes with w~k^2/2, w~n^{2/3}, and pairwise intersections <k have all distances in (k^2,(k+1)^2).
plain: Find the largest set of binary strings of length n in which no two differ in a perfect-square number of positions. Does it grow exponentially in n, and if so at what rate? This is a hypercube version of Sarkozy's theorem on square differences.
math: Let $A(n)=\max\{|C|: C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ d_H(x,y)\notin\{1,4,9,16,\dots\}\ \forall x\ne y\in C\}$. Decide whether $A(n)=2^{o(n)}$. More precisely, determine $\liminf_n\frac1n\log_2A(n)$ and $\limsup_n\frac1n\log_2A(n)$ (in particular whether they are equal).

title: Critical linear firefighter rate on Z^3
credit: Extension of Develin-Hartke (arXiv:math/0409195) and Dyer-Martinez-Pedroza-Thorne (arXiv:1507.03050, Cor. 4); o(t) failure from arXiv:2002.11205.
results: c* >= 8/243 (~0.033), elementary: Loomis-Whitney gives |vertex boundary of B| >= |B|^{2/3}; for c<2a^2-6a^3 with a=2/9, a large initial cube burns forever by induction b_t >= (a(t+T0))^3. Using the asymptotically sharp Wang-Wang vertex isoperimetry (l1-balls, constant 4(3/4)^{2/3}) the same argument heuristically gives ~32/27, not checked rigorously c* <= 8, elementary: protect the l1-sphere |x|_1=D (4D^2+2 vertices) before step D-R; c>8 suffices for large D.
plain: On the 3D grid, a finite fire spreads to all unprotected neighbours each step, and at step t you may protect about ct new vertices. It is known that linear growth is the right order. Elementary arguments show that rate c>8 always contains the fire and that c<8/243 does not. Narrow this gap, or find the exact critical rate.
math: Let c* = inf{c : for every finite initial fire B_0 ⊂ Z^3 there is a protection schedule with at most ⌊c t⌋ newly protected vertices at step t that keeps the total burnt set finite}. Known (QED-derived, elementary): 8/243 ≤ c* ≤ 8 (bound field and W); M additionally records 64/243 ≤ c* ≤ 48/7 (not independently checked here; numerics suggest a static ℓ^4-ball wall gives ≈ 6.4). Target: prove c* > 64/243, i.e. some rate c > 64/243 fails to contain some finite outbreak.

title: Distinct character degrees of the symmetric group
credit: On the irreducible character degrees of symmetric groups and their multiplicities, arXiv:2410.01726 (2024)
premise_risks: arXiv:2410.01726 (preprint, refereeing status unclear): the numerical data for n <= 129 and the suggested limit near 2.5 are context only; Claim does not depend on them.
plain: Conjugate partitions always give representations of S_n of the same dimension, so at most about half of the p(n) irreducible representations can have distinct dimensions. Decide whether the fraction of distinct dimensions tends to a limit, and whether that limit is positive.
math: Let d(n) = #{f^λ : λ ⊢ n} be the number of distinct irreducible character degrees of S_n and p(n) the number of partitions of n. Prove or disprove: d(n)/p(n) converges to a positive limit L as n → ∞.

title: Is the Petersen graph common?
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.20149 (2026 preprint): cited background on common graphs; M does not depend on it.
plain: Color the edges of a huge complete graph red and blue. Does a random coloring minimize the number of single-color copies of the Petersen graph?
math: Let $P$ be the Petersen graph ($10$ vertices, $15$ edges) and $m(P)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{\chi}\frac{\#\{\text{monochromatic copies of }P\text{ in }(K_n,\chi)\}}{\#\{\text{copies of }P\text{ in }K_n\}}$, minimum over red/blue colorings $\chi$ of $E(K_n)$. Is $m(P)=2^{-14}$, i.e. is $P$ common? Equivalently, is $t(P,W)+t(P,1-W)\ge 2^{-14}$ for every graphon $W$? If not, determine $m(P)$.

title: Monochromatic square-sum triangles, many colours
credit: Khalfalah–Szemerédi (2006), monochromatic x+y = z² for finite colourings.
plain: Colour the positive integers with finitely many colours. Show there are always three different numbers of the same colour whose three pairwise sums are all perfect squares.
math: Prove that for every $r\ge1$ and every colouring $\chi:\mathbb N\to\{1,\dots,r\}$ there exist distinct $a,b,c\in\mathbb N$ with $\chi(a)=\chi(b)=\chi(c)$ and $a+b,\ a+c,\ b+c$ all perfect squares. (Equivalently: the triangle hypergraph of the graph on $\mathbb N$ with $a\sim b\iff a+b=\square$ has infinite chromatic number.)

title: Paley spin glass
results: Correct. Q is circulant with eigenvalues chi(a)sqrt p (Gauss sums), so E_p<=p^{3/2}/2. Square-wave ratio is (4/pi^2)sum_{m odd}chi(m)/m^2 + o(1); taking p=1 mod 8 and p=1 mod q for odd q<=y (reciprocity + Dirichlet) gives limsup=1/2. Recomputed p=53881: 0.4925. Bonus: the sum is >=2-pi^2/8 so liminf>=0.31.
plain: Place a ±1 spin at each element of F_p, and let each pair interact through the Legendre symbol of their difference. Equivalently, this is the max-cut problem for the Paley graph. The eigenvalue bound caps the ground-state energy at p^{3/2}/2. Simple square-wave configurations reach this bound along special primes, but heuristic search for typical primes stalls around 0.46. Is the eigenvalue bound asymptotically sharp for all primes?
math: For primes $p\equiv1\pmod4$ let $E_p=\max_{\sigma\in\{\pm1\}^{\mathbb F_p}}\sum_{i<j}\left(\frac{j-i}{p}\right)\sigma_i\sigma_j$. The circulant matrix $Q=\big(\big(\frac{j-i}p\big)\big)_{i,j\in\mathbb F_p}$ is symmetric with eigenvalues $\pm\sqrt p$ (each with multiplicity $\frac{p-1}2$) and $0$, so $E_p\le\frac12p^{3/2}$. (For the Paley graph $P_p$, $\mathrm{surp}(P_p)=\mathrm{maxcut}(P_p)-\frac12|E(P_p)|\le \frac14E_p+\frac p8$.) It is known that $\limsup_p E_p/p^{3/2}=\frac12$: if $(\frac qp)=1$ for all primes $q\le y$, then $\sigma_x=\operatorname{sgn}\cos(2\pi x/p)$ has ratio $\frac12-o_y(1)$; and the same $\sigma$ gives $E_p/p^{3/2}\ge\frac4{\pi^2}\big(2-\frac{\pi^2}8\big)-o(1)\approx0.31$ for every $p$. Determine $\liminf_{p}E_p/p^{3/2}$; in particular, is it $\frac12$?

title: Periodic optimal colourings of Cayley graphs of Z^2
credit: Posed for lattice Cayley graphs in 'The chromatic number of 4-dimensional lattices', arXiv:2407.03513 (2024); related: periodic colourings of quasi-transitive graphs, arXiv:2411.01951 (2024).
results: No proof is claimed. The decidability corollary is correct: compactness (de Bruijn-Erdos) semi-decides chi>k, and enumerating periodic colourings (torus quotients) semi-decides chi<=k if the answer is yes. A Z^2 SFT with one period also has a fully periodic point, so 'periodic point' is unambiguous here.
premise_risks: arXiv:2607.26942 (2026 preprint) is in refs; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Join two points of the integer grid when their difference lies in a fixed finite set D. If this graph can be properly coloured with k colours, can it always be coloured with k colours in a repeating, wallpaper-like pattern? On a line the answer is yes. For some infinite graphs built from trees it is no. The plane is the first open case, and a yes would also give an algorithm for the chromatic number.
math: For finite symmetric $D\subset\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{0\}$ let $G_D=\mathrm{Cay}(\mathbb Z^2,D)$ with $\chi(G_D)=k<\infty$. Must $G_D$ have a proper $k$-colouring invariant under a finite-index subgroup of $\mathbb Z^2$? Equivalently, does the $k$-colouring subshift $X_{D,k}\subset\{1..k\}^{\mathbb Z^2}$ always contain a periodic point? (A yes makes $\{(D,k):\chi(G_D)\le k\}$ decidable via compactness plus enumeration of periodic colourings. A no gives the first weakly aperiodic colouring subshift on $\mathbb Z^2$.) Same question for $\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge3$.

title: The complex of planar graphs
plain: Planar graphs on n labelled vertices form a simplicial complex, because deleting an edge keeps a graph planar. It is pure, since every maximal planar graph has 3n-6 edges. Its homology turns out not to be that of a wedge of top-dimensional spheres: already for n=6 it is concentrated two degrees lower and has 2-torsion. Determine its homology.
math: Let $\Pi_n$ be the simplicial complex on vertex set $E(K_n)$ whose faces are edge sets of planar graphs; it is pure of dimension $3n-7$. Determine $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Z)$, or at least $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Q)$, for all $n$. Known: $\Pi_4$ is a simplex, $\Pi_5=\partial\Delta^9\cong S^8$. For $n=6$ (computed exactly): $\tilde H_*(\Pi_6;\mathbb Q)$ is $\mathbb Q^{15}$ in degree $9=3n-9$ and $0$ elsewhere; $\tilde H_*(\Pi_6;\mathbb F_2)$ is $\mathbb F_2^{15},\mathbb F_2,\mathbb F_2$ in degrees $9,10,11$, so $\tilde H_{10}(\Pi_6;\mathbb Z)$ has $2$-torsion and $\Pi_6$ is not a wedge of spheres. The mod-2 top class is the sum of all triangulations: every face of dimension $3n-8$ of $\Pi_6$ lies in an even number (2 or 4) of facets. Questions: (a) is $\tilde H_*(\Pi_n;\mathbb Q)$ concentrated in degree $3n-9$ for all $n\ge6$, and what is its rank and $S_n$-module structure? (b) Is $\tilde H_{3n-7}(\Pi_n;\mathbb F_2)\ne0$ for all $n\ge5$? Is all torsion 2-torsion?

title: Finding Huang's vertex
results: The PPP-hardness reduction is correct. Take n=m+2. Pad 2^m real pigeons with 2^m+1 dummies, mapped injectively to the 2^m+1 dummy holes. Send the pigeon with C(x)=0 to dummy hole #1, so a collision with dummy #1 decodes to a zero-solution. Embed holes as h -> (h, parity h), which gives even weight. No two even-weight strings are adjacent, so every solution is a collision that decodes to a PIGEON solution.
plain: Huang's theorem says that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours in the set. When the set is listed by a small circuit, how hard is it to find such a corner, or a flaw in the listing? The problem is easily shown to be at least as hard as the pigeonhole class PPP. Is it in PPP, so that it is PPP-complete, or does Huang's linear-algebra proof make it harder?

Is HUANG ∈ PPP (under polynomial-time reductions; or, in the black-box model, is it reducible to PIGEON)? If not, which standard TFNP class contains it, and is it complete for it?
lean_gap: Not formalized: requires circuits, polytime reductions and TFNP classes (PPP), none in Mathlib. Note that 'HUANG ∉ PPP' in the white-box sense implies P ≠ NP-type consequences, so only the positive direction or a black-box separation is realistic.

title: Proof complexity of the sensitivity theorem
plain: Huang proved that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours inside the set. Write this as a propositional formula with one variable per corner. Do polynomial-size proofs exist in resolution, cutting planes or sum-of-squares, measured against the 2^n variables?
math: Let $N=2^n$, $d=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil-1$. $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ is the CNF on variables $x_v$ ($v\in\{0,1\}^n$) plus sequential-counter variables encoding $\sum_v x_v\ge 2^{n-1}+1$, together with the clauses $\neg x_v\vee\bigvee_{u\in U}\neg x_u$ for every $v$ and every $(d+1)$-set $U$ of neighbours of $v$ (size $N\cdot n^{O(\sqrt n)}=N^{1+o(1)}$). It is unsatisfiable by Huang's theorem. Does $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ have refutations of size $N^{O(1)}$ in (a) resolution, (b) cutting planes, (c) sum-of-squares of degree $O(\log N)$? Lower bounds $2^{N^{\Omega(1)}}$ are equally of interest.
lean_gap: Statement left as sorry by design. Reviewer notes that (a) is likely 'no' for matching-type reasons, so W should stress (b),(c).

title: Sparse 3-LPN at noise n^{-1/2}: beating Gaussian elimination

math: Fix k = 3, m = ⌊n^{1.4}⌋ and η = n^{-0.6}. In the 3-sparse LPN problem a secret s ∈ F_2^n is uniform, each sample is (a_i, ⟨a_i,s⟩ + e_i) with a_i uniform among weight-3 vectors of F_2^n and e_i ~ Bernoulli(η) independent, i = 1..m. Prove or disprove: there is a (classical, randomized) algorithm that, given the m samples, outputs s with probability ≥ 2/3 in time exp(o(ηn)) = exp(o(n^{0.4})).

title: Chaos in the double pendulum at every energy
plain: The planar double pendulum with equal masses and equal arms looks chaotic at moderate energies but almost regular at very low and very high energies. Prove that it has genuine (positive-entropy) chaos at every energy above the rest state.
math: Let $H(\theta_1,\theta_2,p_1,p_2)$ be the Hamiltonian of the planar double pendulum with $m_1=m_2=\ell_1=\ell_2=g=1$ on $T^*\mathbb T^2$, with minimum value $E_0$ (the hanging rest state). Prove that for every $E>E_0$ the Hamiltonian flow restricted to $\{H=E\}$ has positive topological entropy.

title: Chaos in the symmetric ABC flow
credit: T. Dombre, U. Frisch, J. M. Greene, M. Henon, A. Mehr, A. M. Soward, 'Chaotic streamlines in the ABC flows', J. Fluid Mech. 167 (1986); V. I. Arnold (1965); M. Henon (1966).

plain: The ABC flow with all three coefficients equal to 1 is the classical steady Euler flow on the 3-torus that is believed to be chaotic. Prove that it really is: show it has positive topological entropy.
math: Prove that the flow of $\dot x=\sin z+\cos y,\ \dot y=\sin x+\cos z,\ \dot z=\sin y+\cos x$ on $\mathbb{T}^3=(\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z})^3$ has positive topological entropy (e.g. by exhibiting a transversal homoclinic orbit to a hyperbolic periodic orbit, or a horseshoe for a Poincare map).

title: Deciding rationality of PL rotation numbers
credit: Belk, Hyde, Moore (2022), arXiv:2211.05825, Questions 3–4.
plain: A circle homeomorphism made of finitely many straight pieces, with rational break points and slopes, has a rotation number. Rational rotation numbers can be confirmed by finding a rational periodic orbit. Irrational ones occur too: Belk–Hyde–Moore found √2−1 with slopes 3/2, 2/3, 1. Is there an algorithm that always decides which case holds?
math: Let $\mathcal P$ be the set of orientation-preserving PL homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ with finitely many rational break points, rational slopes and $f(0)\in\mathbb Q$, encoded by these data. Is $\{f\in\mathcal P:\rho(f)\in\mathbb Q\}$ decidable? (It is computably enumerable: if $\rho(f)=p/q$, the zero set of the lift $F^q(x)-x-p$ is a nonempty finite union of rational points and rational intervals.)

title: Ergodicity of the regular tetrahedron billiard
plain: A billiard ball bounces inside a regular tetrahedron. The tetrahedron does not tile space, and its dihedral angle arccos(1/3) is an irrational multiple of pi. So the billiard cannot be unfolded into a straight-line flow on a torus or a translation structure. Is the motion ergodic, so that almost every trajectory equidistributes in position and direction?
math: Let $\Delta\subset\mathbb R^3$ be a regular tetrahedron and $\phi_t$ the billiard flow on the unit tangent bundle $T^1\Delta$, with specular reflection at faces and orbits hitting edges or vertices discarded (a null set). Prove or disprove that $\phi_t$ is ergodic with respect to Liouville measure.

title: From density to Kolmogorov typicality of positive entropy in symplectic families
credit: P. Berger and D. Turaev, arXiv:2507.11375 (2025), Thm B; P. Berger, arXiv:2003.09329 (Kolmogorov typicality / emergence).

plain: Berger and Turaev showed that families of area-preserving surface maps having positive metric entropy at every parameter are dense among smooth families. Show this is typical, i.e. holds for a Kolmogorov-generic (prevalent) set of families, or find a robust obstruction.
math: Fix a compact surface Σ with area form ω and k ≥ 1. Let F be the space of C^∞ families (f_p)_{p∈[0,1]^k} of ω-preserving diffeomorphisms of Σ (C^∞ topology on (p,x) ↦ f_p(x)) such that f_p has an elliptic periodic point for every p, and let F_+ = {families with h_Leb(f_p) > 0 for Lebesgue-a.e. p}. Prove or disprove: F_+ contains a Baire-generic (countable intersection of open dense) subset of an open set U ⊂ F on which Berger-Turaev's density theorem applies; equivalently disprove by exhibiting a nonempty open U ⊂ F such that for every family in a dense subset of U, {p : h_Leb(f_p) = 0} has positive Lebesgue measure. (Here 'Kolmogorov typical' must be replaced by the exact notion in Berger-Turaev, arXiv:2507.11375, if it differs from Baire genericity in the family space.)
lean_gap: Not formalized: needs C^∞ family spaces of symplectic surface diffeomorphisms, Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy, and the Berger-Turaev typicality notion. The M_fix's genericity notion should be verified against arXiv:2507.11375 before use.

title: Integrability of the egg-crate torus
credit: V. V. Kozlov, non-integrability of perturbed geodesic flows on the torus (Poincaré-Kozlov theory; 'Symmetries, Topology and Resonances in Hamiltonian Mechanics', 1996); Paternain, Taimanov for entropy obstructions
plain: Put the surface z = ε sin x sin y over a flat square torus. Show its geodesic flow is never integrable, however small the bumps are.
math: For $\varepsilon>0$ let $g_\varepsilon$ be the metric on $\mathbb T^2=\mathbb R^2/(2\pi\mathbb Z)^2$ induced from the graph $z=\varepsilon\sin x\sin y$, i.e. $g_\varepsilon=dx^2+dy^2+\varepsilon^2(\cos x\sin y\,dx+\sin x\cos y\,dy)^2$. Prove that for every $\varepsilon>0$ the geodesic flow on $T^*\mathbb T^2\setminus0$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of the Hamiltonian (for example, by showing positive topological entropy).

title: Is the Mandelbrot set decidable at Gaussian rationals?
credit: P. Potgieter, arXiv:cs/0604003 (2006), Sec. 2.3.
results: The reduction is correct apart from one flaw. A non-repelling cycle implies c in M, since by Fatou all cycles are repelling when c is outside M. The example arithmetic checks out: mu/2-mu^2/4=(37+16i)/100. But (*) as stated is FALSE. c=-2 and c=+-i are Gaussian-integer Misiurewicz parameters in M with all cycles repelling (c=i: 0->i->-1+i->-i->-1+i). The fix excludes Z[i], where membership is a finite check.
plain: Is there an algorithm that takes a complex number with rational real and imaginary parts and decides whether it lies in the Mandelbrot set? Escaping points can be confirmed, and so can points that have an attracting or neutral cycle of some period, since for each period that is an exact algebraic check. The trouble is points on the boundary where every cycle repels. No such Gaussian rational is known, but none has been ruled out.
math: Let $M=\{c\in\mathbb C:(f_c^{n}(0))_{n\ge0}\text{ bounded}\}$, $f_c(z)=z^2+c$. Prove or disprove that $M\cap\mathbb Q(i)$ is a decidable subset of $\mathbb Q(i)$. $\mathbb Q(i)\setminus M$ is r.e. For each $n$, the existence of an $n$-cycle with multiplier of modulus $\le1$ is decidable for algebraic $c$ (Tarski), and such a cycle forces $c\in M$. $M\cap\mathbb Z[i]$ is a finite, explicitly computable set (it contains the Misiurewicz points $-2,\pm i$, whose cycles are all repelling). So a positive answer would follow from (*): every $c\in(M\cap\mathbb Q(i))\setminus\mathbb Z[i]$ has a non-repelling cycle. Prove or disprove (*). (Example: $c=(37+16i)/100$ lies on the main cardioid with multiplier $(3+4i)/5$, a Siegel parameter.)

title: Is the measure of the hyperbolic real quadratic parameters computable?
results: Checked: λ(H) is lower semicomputable. Each CE(C,γ) piece is an intersection of finite-time conditions, so it is only upper semicomputable, which is the wrong direction. The 'equivalently' clause is valid through Lyubich's regular-or-stochastic theorem and Avila–Moreira (almost every stochastic parameter is CE).
premise_risks: arXiv 2505.20495 (Golmakani–Koudjinan–Luzzatto–Pilarczyk, 2025 preprint): cited only for the remark that computer-assisted schemes certify expansion, not measure; statement does not depend on it.
plain: For real c between −2 and 1/4, the map x ↦ x²+c has an attracting cycle for an open dense set of c, yet the chaotic parameters have positive length (Jakobson). Is the total length of the parameters with an attracting cycle a computable number? It can be approximated from below by listing windows, but no known method approximates it from above.
math: Let $H=\{c\in[-2,1/4]:\ x\mapsto x^2+c\text{ has an attracting periodic orbit}\}$. Is the Lebesgue measure $\lambda(H)$ a computable real number? ($H$ is open and its components can be certified by interval arithmetic, so $\lambda(H)$ is lower semicomputable; Jakobson's theorem gives $\lambda(H)<9/4$.) Equivalently: is the measure of the set of stochastic (Collet–Eckmann) parameters lower semicomputable?

title: Outer billiards around analytic tables with flat points
credit: Moser's boundedness question (J. Moser, Stable and Random Motions, 1973); Douady (thesis, 1982); Sorrentino arXiv:2610.06418 (2026) for the C^1-generic case.

At a flat point of order k the radius of curvature satisfies rho(theta)~|theta|^{-k/(k+1)} (|theta|^{-2/3} for x^4+y^4), and the tangency point q(p) is only C^{1/(k+1)} across the tangent lines at the flat points. So T and the limiting map at infinity are genuinely non-smooth, and KAM does not apply directly. The claim is correct.
premise_risks: arXiv:2610.06418 (Sorrentino, 2026 preprint): cited for C^1-generic unbounded orbits (centrally symmetric tables only); motivation only, the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Outer billiards around a smooth convex shape with positive curvature has only bounded orbits (Moser-Douady). Polygons, semicircles and generic C^1 shapes can have orbits that escape to infinity. What if the table is analytic and strictly convex, but its curvature vanishes at a few points, like the superellipse x^4+y^4 ≤ 1? Decide whether every orbit stays bounded.
math: Let $K\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a strictly convex body whose boundary is a real-analytic closed curve with curvature vanishing at at least one point (hence, by analyticity, at finitely many). For $p\in\mathbb R^2\setminus K$, let $T(p)=2q-p$, where $q\in\partial K$ is the tangency point of the tangent line from $p$ that has $K$ on its left. Is every $T$-orbit bounded, for every such $K$? If not, characterize the $K$ with unbounded orbits, e.g. by the vanishing orders of the curvature or by symmetry. First test case: $K=\{x^4+y^4\le1\}$.

title: Three identical vortices on a square torus are chaotic
credit: Borisov, Mamaev, Kilin, Regul. Chaotic Dyn. (2019); survey arXiv:2003.00716 (Thm 7); Stremler-Aref (1999, chao-dyn/9907038) for the zero-circulation integrable case
plain: On a flat torus, three point vortices with total circulation zero form an integrable system (Stremler-Aref), but for vortices of equal strength even three are believed chaotic, from numerics only. Prove that three identical point vortices on the square torus are not integrable; the same question is open for four.
math: Let $G$ be the Green function of $\mathbb T=\mathbb C/(\mathbb Z+i\mathbb Z)$ ($\Delta G=\delta_0-1$) and $H=-\sum_{i<j}G(z_i-z_j)$ on $\{(z_1,\dots,z_N)\in\mathbb T^N: z_i\ne z_j\}$ with symplectic form $\sum_i dx_i\wedge dy_i$. The centre $Z=\sum_i z_i\in\mathbb T$ is conserved; the reduced space $M_N=\{Z=Z_0\}/(\tfrac1N\mathbb Z[i]/\mathbb Z[i])$ is symplectic of dimension $2N-2$. Prove that for $N=3$ the reduced flow on $M_3$ has no real-analytic first integral functionally independent of $H$ (and likewise for $N=4$ on $M_4$).

title: A monotile that forces quasicrystalline symmetry
credit: Einstein problem: Socolar-Taylor (2011, arXiv:1009.1419); Smith-Myers-Kaplan-Goodman-Strauss (2023, arXiv:2303.10798); Gummelt decagon covering (1996); Steinhardt-Jeong quasi-unit-cell model
plain: Every aperiodic monotile known (Socolar-Taylor, the hat, the spectre, and the 3D examples) has tilings with only crystallographic rotational structure: 2-, 3-, 4- or 6-fold. Is there a single tile in the plane whose tilings are all forced to be quasicrystalline with fivefold symmetry, as Penrose tilings are? Or is non-crystallographic symmetry something only two or more tiles can enforce?
math: Call a compact set T ⊂ ℝ² homeomorphic to a closed disc a monotile if it tiles ℝ² by isometric copies, reflections allowed. Does there exist a monotile T such that (i) every tiling by copies of T uses only finitely many orientations of T (up to translation), and (ii) for every such tiling 𝒯 the translation hull Ω(𝒯), the closure of {𝒯 + v} in the standard local topology (agreement on B(0,1/ε) after a translation of size < ε), is invariant under rotation by 2π/5? (Equivalently, the rotated tiling R𝒯 lies in Ω(𝒯).) The R³ icosahedral analogue is a secondary target.

title: A strongly aperiodic monotile in four dimensions
credit: Kamenetsky 2026, arXiv:2610.00916, Problem 9.1 (context: Smith-Myers-Kaplan-Goodman-Strauss 2023, arXiv:2303.10798; Tsiokos 2026, arXiv:2609.19214)

math: Find a compact set $T\subset\mathbb R^4$ homeomorphic to a closed 4-ball such that (i) $\mathbb R^4$ admits a tiling by isometric copies of $T$ (reflections allowed; copies cover $\mathbb R^4$ with pairwise disjoint interiors), and (ii) no such tiling is invariant under any nonzero translation. (Drop the weak variant (ii'), or flag it as possibly easy via prisms over a 3D monotile.)

title: Beat the (1-o(1)) log2 d exponent in quasi-polynomial polytope diameter bounds
credit: Kalai-Kleitman 1992; Todd 2014 (arXiv:1402.3579); Sukegawa; Liu-Ge-Ye 2026 (arXiv:2609.33434)

plain: All known bounds on the diameter of a d-dimensional polyhedron with n facets have the form (n−d)^{log₂ d − O(log log d)}. The latest (Liu–Ge–Ye 2026) is (n−d)^{log₂ G_d} with G_d ~ (4 ln 2) d/(ln d)². Get an exponent at most (1−ε) log₂ d.
math: Let $\Delta_u(d,n)$ be the maximum graph diameter of a pointed $d$-polyhedron with $n$ facets. Known: $\Delta_u(d,n)\le (n-d)^{\log_2 G_d}$, $G_d=(4\ln2+o(1))d/(\ln d)^2$ (Liu–Ge–Ye 2026), after Kalai–Kleitman, Todd, Sukegawa. Prove $\Delta_u(d,n)\le (n-d)^{(1-\varepsilon)\log_2 d}$ for some fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and all large $d$.

title: Cross-polytopes in 4D
credit: Klee & Wagon, Old and New Unsolved Problems in Plane Geometry and Number Theory (1991), Problem 11.5; V. V. Makeev (d = 3); R. Karasev, arXiv:0905.2671 (2009).

title: Geodesic squares on convex surfaces
credit: Toeplitz 1911 (square peg problem); Schnirelmann 1944 (smooth case); constant-curvature surfaces: arXiv:2507.07945 (Naseri Sadr 2025)

plain: On a smooth convex surface, measure distance by the length of the shortest path on the surface. Every smooth simple closed curve on the surface should contain four points that form a 'square' in this sense: four equal sides and two equal diagonals.

Prove that every smooth simple closed curve $\gamma\subset S$ contains four distinct points $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, in this cyclic order along $\gamma$, with $d(p_1,p_2)=d(p_2,p_3)=d(p_3,p_4)=d(p_4,p_1)>0$ and $d(p_1,p_3)=d(p_2,p_4)$.

title: Gromov width of the 4D l^4 ball

Prove or disprove: c_G(U) = c0 (i.e. U satisfies the strong Viterbo equality between Gromov width and cylindrical capacity).

If T_n is near T_0 the linear part is near a symmetry ±R_u; q*conj(u) cannot be real (primitivity / 2*3^n not a square), so its vector part has length >=1/2 while |q u| <= sqrt2*3^{n/2}, giving rotation error >> 3^{-n/2}.
premise_risks: QED-internal derivation (unrefereed): the bounds 1/12 ≤ κ ≤ 1/2 (Hurwitz-order primitivity checked by computer only to n = 11). The formal Claim only uses the definitions, not these bounds.
plain: Glue regular tetrahedra face to face in a chain of length n; it can never close exactly. How close to closing can it get? Short arguments show the best gap is at least about 3^{-n/2} and, for infinitely many n, at most about 3^{-n/12}; counting suggests 3^{-n/6}. Narrow the exponent range [1/12, 1/2].
math: Let g(k) be the minimal Hausdorff distance between T_k and T_0 over non-backtracking face-reflection chains of length k, and κ := liminf_{n→∞} −(1/n) log₃ min_{1≤k≤n} g(k). Known: 1/12 ≤ κ ≤ 1/2 (heuristic κ = 1/6). Prove κ > 1/12, i.e. there are δ > 0 and N such that for every n ≥ N some non-backtracking chain of length between 1 and n ends within 3^{−(1/12+δ)n} of T_0.

title: Sofa stability
credit: Baek (2024), 'Optimality of Gerver's Sofa', arXiv:2411.19826.
premise_risks: arXiv:2411.19826 (Baek 2024; refereeing status unclear): the problem assumes Gerver's sofa is the maximizer. The formal Claim avoids this by quantifying over an unspecified stable sofa G, so it does not depend on Baek's result.
arXiv:2610.13955 (2026 preprint, cited in refs): context only; nothing in the statement depends on it.
plain: Baek (2024) proved that Gerver's sofa has the largest area among shapes that can be moved around a right-angled corner in a hallway of width 1. Show that any movable sofa whose area is nearly Gerver's must be nearly Gerver's sofa in shape (which in particular gives uniqueness).
math: A moving sofa is a compact connected $S\subset\mathbb R^2$ that can be moved by a continuous rigid motion from $(-\infty,0]\times[0,1]$ to $[0,1]\times(-\infty,0]$ inside $L=((-\infty,1]\times[0,1])\cup([0,1]\times(-\infty,1])$. Let $G$ be Gerver's sofa, of area $A_G\approx2.21953$. Prove that there are $C,\alpha>0$ such that every moving sofa $S$ with $|S|\ge A_G-\varepsilon$ satisfies $\min_{g}|gS\,\triangle\,G|\le C\varepsilon^{\alpha}$, the minimum over rigid motions $g$ of the plane.

title: Superlinear unit distances on the unit sphere
credit: Erdős, Hickerson, Pach, 'A problem of Leo Moser about repeated distances on the sphere', Amer. Math. Monthly 96 (1989); Swanepoel-Valtr (2004)
plain: In 2026 a number-field construction showed that points in the plane can have n^(1+c) unit distances, disproving Erdos's conjecture. On a sphere of radius 1/sqrt2 an n^(4/3) construction is classical, but on the unit sphere only n·sqrt(log n) is known. Can the new ideas give a power gain there?
math: Prove or disprove: there is $c>0$ such that for infinitely many $n$ there exist $P\subset S^2=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^3:|x|=1\}$ with $|P|=n$ and $\#\{\{p,q\}\subset P:|p-q|=1\}\ge n^{1+c}$.

title: An explicit, checkable counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture
premise_risks: OpenAI October 2026 release (Family 157), surveyed in arXiv:2610.17090 (unrefereed): the claim that Hadwiger's conjecture is false at all. If that disproof is wrong, the problem asks for something that may not exist, and its whole motivation collapses.
arXiv:2609.35361 and arXiv:2606.01586 (2026 preprints): background on the α ≤ 2 / connected-matching route and the size of known counterexamples.
plain: Hadwiger's conjecture says a graph that needs t colours contains the complete graph K_t as a minor. A disproof claimed in October 2026 (not yet peer reviewed) is non-constructive: it uses graphs with no three pairwise non-adjacent vertices, on roughly 2^(10^12) vertices or more, and never names a graph. Find one concrete graph on fewer than a million vertices for which the conjecture fails, with a proof that can be checked.
math: For a finite graph $G$ let $h(G)=\max\{t: K_t\preceq G\}$ be its Hadwiger number and $\chi(G)$ its chromatic number. Exhibit an explicit graph $G$ with $|V(G)|<10^6$ and $h(G)<\chi(G)$, with a complete proof of both bounds that can be checked (by hand or by a computer computation of feasible size). Sufficient route (Cambie): an explicit $G$ with $\alpha(G)\le2$, $|V(G)|=4t-1$ and no connected matching of size $t$ (a matching whose edges are pairwise joined by an edge of $G$) violates Hadwiger's conjecture.

title: Graceful labellings of forests
credit: Relaxation of the Ringel–Kotzig–Rosa Graceful Tree Conjecture; related: Van Bussel (EJC 2002, range-relaxed graceful labellings), Adamaszek–Allen–Grosu–Hladký arXiv:1608.01577, gracesize arXiv:2511.11331.
plain: A forest with m edges and c trees has m + c vertices. Label them with 0, 1, ..., m + c - 1, each label used once, so that the m edge differences |label(u) - label(v)| are all different. Show that every forest has such a labelling. The case 'a tree plus one isolated vertex' already says that every tree can be labelled gracefully if one spare label is allowed.
math: Prove that every forest $F$ with $m$ edges and $c\ge1$ components has a bijection $\ell:V(F)\to\{0,1,\dots,m+c-1\}$ such that the values $|\ell(u)-\ell(v)|$, $uv\in E(F)$, are pairwise distinct. (Key special case: $F=T\sqcup K_1$, i.e. every tree with $m$ edges has an injective labelling into $\{0,\dots,m+1\}$ with distinct edge differences.)

title: Ringel for forests
credit: Ringel (1963); Montgomery-Pokrovskiy-Sudakov (arXiv:2001.02665); Keevash-Staden (arXiv:2004.09947); Barrientos-Minion, EJGTA 4(2) 2016 (ρ-labelled forests)
plain: Ringel's conjecture, now a theorem for large n, says the complete graph on 2m+1 vertices splits into 2m+1 copies of any tree with m edges. Show the same holds for every forest with m edges. A stronger form asks that every such forest have a rho-labelling, which gives a cyclic decomposition.
math: Prove that for every m ≥ 1 and every forest F with m edges and no isolated vertices, E(K_{2m+1}) can be partitioned into 2m+1 subgraphs each isomorphic to F. Stronger form: every such F admits a ρ-labelling.

title: Computable connective constants
plain: Count the self-avoiding walks of length n on the Cayley graph of a finitely generated group. Their n-th roots decrease to the connective constant, so it can always be approximated from above. For groups with a solvable word problem, can it always be computed to any precision, i.e. also approximated from below?
math: Let $G$ be a finitely generated group with solvable word problem, $S=S^{-1}$ a finite generating set, $c_n$ the number of $n$-step self-avoiding walks from $e$ in $\mathrm{Cay}(G,S)$, and $\mu(G,S)=\lim_n c_n^{1/n}=\inf_n c_n^{1/n}$ (a right-computable real). Is $\mu(G,S)$ always a computable real? If not, construct $(G,S)$ with solvable word problem and $\mu(G,S)$ non-computable. If so, is the map (word-problem algorithm, $S$) $\mapsto\mu(G,S)$ uniformly computable?

title: Deciding limit cycles
credit: Extension of Graca-Zhong (arXiv:2101.07701) noncomputability of planar periodic orbits; related: Hilbert's 16th problem, Il'yashenko on algebraic unsolvability of the center-focus problem.
results: The claim that hyperbolic limit cycles are r.e. via interval certification is correct. The remark that fixed-degree versions 'can become trivially decidable' is wrong. Each fixed-degree set is still infinite. Bautin's finite generation only gives non-uniform decidability of the local center condition, not of whether cycles exist.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.22058 (2026 preprint): cited only for the claim that the planar (N=2) case is open and that Lyapunov stability is undecidable in dimension 5; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: Given a polynomial vector field in the plane with rational coefficients, is there an algorithm that decides whether it has a limit cycle, that is, an isolated closed orbit? Hilbert's 16th problem asks how many limit cycles there can be. This asks only whether their existence is algorithmically decidable. The same question can be asked for closed orbits of any kind, including those in period annuli around centres.
math: Let $\mathcal L=\{(P,Q)\in\mathbb Q[x,y]^2:\ \dot x=P,\dot y=Q$ has a limit cycle, i.e. a non-constant periodic orbit that has a neighbourhood containing no other periodic orbit$\}$ and $\mathcal P=\{(P,Q):$ the system has a non-constant periodic orbit in $\mathbb R^2\}$, with inputs given by their rational coefficient lists (degree unbounded). (a) Is $\mathcal L$ decidable? (b) Is $\mathcal P$ decidable? (c) Are $\mathcal L,\mathcal P$ or their complements recursively enumerable? (d) Same questions restricted to degree 2.

title: First-order convergence law for random Latin squares
results: Caution: route (i) as originally proposed has a flaw. The extension property 'every finite partial configuration extends in every consistent way w.h.p.' is false. A new x with x∘a1=b1 and x∘a2=b2 has expected count n·n^{-2}→0, because x∘a=b already determines x. The structure is functionally sparse (Lynch-type), not G(n,1/2)-type, so the route was rewritten.
premise_risks: arXiv:2606.18174 (Allsop-Morris, 2026 preprint): cited only as evidence that even the Poisson(1) idempotent law is unproved; the statement assumes nothing from it.
plain: Pick a Latin square of order n uniformly at random and read it as a multiplication table x∘y on n symbols. Does every first-order statement about this table have a limiting probability as n grows? A zero-one law fails: the number of x with x∘x=x should be asymptotically Poisson(1), so the probability that one exists should tend to 1−1/e rather than 0 or 1.
math: Let $L_n$ be uniform among Latin squares on $[n]$ and $\mathcal Q_n=([n],\circ)$ with $x\circ y=L_n(x,y)$. Prove or disprove: for every first-order sentence $\varphi$ in the language $\{\circ,=\}$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr[\mathcal Q_n\models\varphi]$ exists. (A 0-1 law should fail: by symbol-relabelling symmetry, $\mathbb E\#\{x:x\circ x=x\}=1$ exactly, and this count is conjecturally Poisson(1).) Expected route, as for Lynch's random unary functions: (i) w.h.p. the bounded-depth term closure of any bounded tuple is free except for coincidences counted by balanced configurations ($v$ elements, $v$ independent equations); (ii) a joint Poisson limit for the counts of all such balanced configurations, e.g. cycles of $x\mapsto x\circ x$. A disproof would need a definable sparse statistic with no limit law.

title: Hat Ising universality
credit: Hat tiling: Smith, Myers, Kaplan, Goodman-Strauss (2023); numerics on hat-tiling Ising models as cited in the notes (arXiv:2402.11331, arXiv:2307.11054); background: Chelkak-Smirnov universality on isoradial graphs.
plain: Magnets on a hat tiling should behave at their critical point exactly like magnets on a square grid. Prove it.
math: Let G be the tile-adjacency graph of a hat tiling T in the hull. Prove: there is β_c ∈ (0,∞), the same for all T in the hull, such that (a) for β > β_c the plus-state magnetization at a tile satisfies c(β−β_c)^{1/8} ≤ M_T(β) ≤ C(β−β_c)^{1/8} uniformly in the tile, and M_T(β) = 0 for β ≤ β_c; (b) for β < β_c the susceptibility χ(β) = sup over tiles x of Σ_y ⟨σ_xσ_y⟩_β satisfies χ(β) ≍ (β_c−β)^{−7/4}; (c) for β < β_c the correlation length ξ(β), defined by −lim inf_{|x−y|→∞} log⟨σ_xσ_y⟩/|x−y| = 1/ξ, satisfies ξ(β) ≍ (β_c−β)^{−1}; all for β in a neighbourhood of β_c.
lean_gap: Not formalized: needs hat tiling construction, infinite-volume Ising Gibbs states, and definitions of M, χ, ξ.

title: Irrationality of the quartic oscillator ground state
plain: The lowest energy of the quartic oscillator, -d^2/dx^2 + x^4 on the line, is about 1.0603620905. Show that it is irrational.
math: Let $E_0=\min\sigma\big(-\tfrac{d^2}{dx^2}+x^4\big)$, the operator taken self-adjoint on $L^2(\mathbb R)$ ($E_0=1.06036209048418\ldots$). Prove that $E_0\notin\mathbb Q$.

title: Spikes at the squares
credit: Cheon, Exner, Šeba (2000), arXiv:quant-ph/0004058 (continuum analogue with spikes at the squares).
results: Correct with a caveat. The spike gaps are 2m+1, so the spike-to-spike map is C·R(k(2m+1)), a one-frequency analytic cocycle over rotation by 2k. Herman's subharmonicity gives L ≥ log|C_11| = log sqrt(1+λ²/(4sin²k)). This bounds the phase-averaged exponent only: at the fixed phase θ=k (coupled to the frequency) the limit is not guaranteed, so eigenfunction decay is heuristic.
plain: On the half-line lattice, add a fixed spike of height λ at every perfect square. The free band (-2,2) then has no absolutely continuous spectrum, by Remling's theorem. Decide whether the spectrum inside the band is pure point (localized states) or singular continuous. A heuristic in the physics literature predicts singular continuous.
math: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\,\mathbf 1_{\{m^2:m\ge1\}}(n)\,u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$, $u(0)=0$, $\lambda\ne0$ fixed, and let $\mu$ be the spectral measure of $\delta_1$. Determine the spectral type of $\mu|_{(-2,2)}$: is it pure point, purely singular continuous, or mixed? (Known: $\mu_{ac}=0$ by Remling's theorem. Cheon–Exner–Šeba heuristically predict purely singular continuous spectrum for the continuum analogue; positive Lyapunov exponents of the spike-to-spike cocycle suggest pure point.)

title: Ten Martini for every periodic planar lattice
credit: Extends Avila–Jitomirskaya (Ten Martini, Annals 2009) and Becker–Han–Jitomirskaya–Zworski (honeycomb, arXiv:1803.00988).
results: The pendant-twin counterexample is correct. Attach two pendant vertices x,x' to each vertex of Z^2. Then delta_x - (phase) delta_x' is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 0 for every B. For E nonzero, E is in sigma iff E-2/E is in sigma(H_sq), which lies in [-4,4]. So a punctured neighbourhood of 0 is a gap, 0 is isolated, and the naive statement fails.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.15812 (2026 preprint): 1D Robust Ten Martini; cited as a possible tool only, M does not depend on it.
arXiv:2611.10767 (2026 preprint): cited; M does not depend on it.
plain: A tight-binding electron on any doubly periodic planar network in a uniform magnetic field: is the energy spectrum always a Cantor set when the flux per cell is irrational? This is known for the square lattice (Ten Martini), the honeycomb lattice and the Lieb lattice, each by a reduction to a one-dimensional operator. Flat-band eigenvalues that persist in any field can sit isolated, so they must be set aside. The question is whether what remains is always a Cantor set, or at least never contains an interval.
math: Let $G\subset\mathbb R^2$ be a connected planar graph with straight edges that is invariant under a lattice $L\cong\mathbb Z^2$ and has finitely many $L$-orbits of vertices. For a constant field $B$ with vector potential $A$, set $(H_B\psi)(x)=\sum_{y\sim x}e^{i\int_{[x,y]}A}\psi(y)$ on $\ell^2(V(G))$, and let $2\pi\alpha=B\cdot\mathrm{covol}(L)$. Let $\Sigma'$ be the derived set of $\sigma(H_B)$, i.e. $\sigma(H_B)$ minus its isolated points (eigenvalues of infinite multiplicity, i.e. flat bands). Prove or disprove: for every such $G$ and every irrational $\alpha$, $\Sigma'$ is a nonempty Cantor set. At minimum, decide whether $\sigma(H_B)$ is always nowhere dense. The first open instance is the kagome lattice in a uniform field. (The pure line-graph flux pattern, with no flux through the triangles, reduces to the honeycomb case.)

title: Break the 5/8 barrier for primes with triply well-factorable weights
credit: A. Pascadi, arXiv:2505.00653 (2025), Thm 1.3 and remarks on the 5/8 limit; J. D. Lichtman, arXiv:2309.08522 (2023); triply well-factorable weights from Maynard's equidistribution papers.
premise_risks: arXiv:2505.00653 (Pascadi, 2025 preprint, refereeing status unverified): the known baseline θ* ≥ 5/8 unconditionally and the exact definition of triply well-factorable weights (Def 1.1) are taken from it.
arXiv:2602.20917 and arXiv:2608.13299 (2026 preprints): used only to check that no one has passed 5/8; the statement assumes nothing from them.
plain: The primes are known to be evenly spread over residue classes, on average over moduli up to x^{5/8}, if the average is weighted by triply well-factorable weights. Push the exponent past 5/8, or show the dispersion method cannot.
math: Say (lambda_q)_{q<=Q} is triply well-factorable of level Q if for all Q1Q2Q3=Q there are 1-bounded alpha,beta,gamma supported on q_i<=Q_i with lambda=alpha*beta*gamma (Dirichlet convolution). Let theta* = sup of theta such that for all eps,A>0, fixed a!=0, and every such lambda of level Q=x^{theta-eps}: sum_{q<=Q,(q,a)=1} lambda_q(pi(x;q,a)-pi(x)/phi(q)) <<_{eps,A,a} x(log x)^{-A}. Known theta*>=5/8 (Pascadi). Prove theta*>5/8.

title: Close the gap in the density of integers that are sums of two rational cubes
credit: Alpöge, Bhargava, Shnidman, Integers expressible as the sum of two rational cubes, arXiv:2210.10730 (2022); Koymans-Smith arXiv:2606.06024 (2026) for the complement side.
premise_risks: arXiv:2606.06024 (Koymans-Smith, 2026 preprint): source of the 31.95% (0.3195) lower bound for non-sums; the formalized Claim does not use it, but the stated M does.
plain: BSD plus the minimalist rank heuristic predict that exactly half of all integers are sums of two rational cubes. Proven: at least 2/21 are (Alpöge–Bhargava–Shnidman), and at least 31.95% are not (Koymans–Smith). Improve either bound.
math: Let $\mathcal S=\{n\in\mathbb Z: n=x^3+y^3,\ x,y\in\mathbb Q\}$ and $d_\pm$ the lower densities of $\mathcal S$ and of its complement (ordered by $|n|$). Known: $\underline d(\mathcal S)\ge 2/21$, $\underline d(\mathcal S^c)\ge 0.3195$. Conjecture: both densities equal $1/2$. Improve either constant.

title: Do GRH and Elliott–Halberstam together refute the Alternative Hypothesis?
credit: Baluyot, Goldston, Suriajaya, Turnage-Butterbaugh, The Alternative Hypothesis for zeros of the Riemann zeta-function, arXiv:2508.10857 (2025); Goldston et al., arXiv:2507.06823; Lagarias–Rodgers arXiv:1905.12123.
premise_risks: arXiv:2508.10857 (2025 preprint, unrefereed as far as known): the problem takes its precise definition of AH, and the claimed explicit limit of F(α) under RH + AH, from this paper.
arXiv:2507.06823 (2025 preprint): background on F(α) under AH.
plain: The Alternative Hypothesis says normalized gaps between zeta zeros are almost all near half-integers. It contradicts GUE, but no proven hypothesis is known to rule it out. Decide whether GRH plus Elliott–Halberstam (strong statements about primes, not zeros) is incompatible with it.
math: Let AH be as in arXiv:2508.10857. Does RH + GRH for Dirichlet L-functions + the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture (or GEH) imply that AH fails? (The 'equivalently' clause is a research route, not an equivalent statement, and is dropped.)
lean_gap: Not formalized: needs zeta-zero enumeration, pair correlation, EH.

title: Improve H_1 <= 12 under EH alone
credit: D.H.J. Polymath 2014, arXiv:1407.4897; J. Maynard 2015, arXiv:1311.4600
plain: Assuming Elliott–Halberstam, Maynard's sieve gives infinitely many pairs of primes at distance at most 12. The generalized conjecture GEH gives 6. Lower 12 using EH alone.
math: Let $H_1=\liminf_{n}(p_{n+1}-p_n)$. Assuming EH (level $\theta=1-\varepsilon$ for all $\varepsilon>0$, for the von Mangoldt function only, not GEH), prove $H_1\le 10$, or prove that no Selberg/Maynard-type sieve weight using EH alone can give $H_1<12$.

title: Interval-sieve extremal bounds behind the Banks–Ford–Tao gap prediction
credit: Banks, Ford, Tao, Large prime gaps and probabilistic models, Invent. Math. 2023 (arXiv:1908.08613)
plain: Banks, Ford and Tao showed that a random sieve model of the primes predicts the largest prime gap below x is about g(ξ log²x), where g is controlled by an extremal sieve quantity W_y. W_y is the fewest survivors in [0,y] after one residue class is removed for each prime up to √(y/log y). Narrow the bounds on W_y.
math: Let W_y = min over residue choices (a_p) of #{n ∈ [0,y] ∩ ℤ : n ≢ a_p (mod p) for all primes p <= (y/log y)^{1/2}}. Known (Banks-Ford-Tao): (4+o(1)) y log log y/log^2 y <= W_y <= y/log y + O(y log log y/log^2 y). Prove or disprove: there is an absolute c > 0 with W_y >= c·y/log y for all sufficiently large y.

title: Largest prime factor of Markov numbers
credit: Extends Corvaja–Zannier, 'On the greatest prime factor of Markov pairs', Rend. Sem. Mat. Univ. Padova 116 (2006).
plain: Markov numbers are the numbers appearing in positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Show that the largest prime factor of a Markov number tends to infinity. Equivalently, for any finite set of primes, only finitely many Markov numbers are built from those primes alone.
math: Let $\mathcal M=\{m\ge1:\exists\,x,y\in\mathbb Z_{>0},\ x^2+y^2+m^2=3xym\}$ and let $P(m)$ denote the largest prime factor of $m$ (with $P(1)=1$). Prove that $P(m)\to\infty$ as $m\to\infty$ in $\mathcal M$; equivalently, for every finite set $S$ of primes, only finitely many $m\in\mathcal M$ are $S$-units.

title: Lower the exponent 0.7785 for A4-quartic fields
credit: Bhargava, Shankar, Taniguchi, Thorne, Tsimerman, Zhao, 'Bounds on 2-torsion in class groups of number fields and integral points on elliptic curves', JAMS 2020 (arXiv:1701.02458, Thm 1.4); Loughran-Paterson arXiv:2510.05248
premise_risks: arXiv:2510.05248 (Loughran-Paterson, 2025 preprint): lower bound X^{1/2} log X and the statement that 0.7784... is the current record; the Claim itself depends only on the refereed BSTTTZ exponent.
arXiv:2602.23619 (Alberts-Bucur, 2026 preprint): cited only for the status 'no 2026 improvement'.
plain: Malle predicts about X^{1/2} log X quartic fields with Galois group A4 and discriminant up to X. Loughran–Paterson (2025) proved the matching lower bound. The best upper bound is still about X^{0.7785}. Lower the exponent.
math: Let N_{A4}(X) count quartic L/Q with Gal(L~/Q)=A4 and |Delta_L|<=X. Known: X^{1/2} log X << N_{A4}(X) << X^{0.7784...+eps} (Loughran-Paterson arXiv:2510.05248 Thm 1.1; BSTTTZ JAMS 2020 Thm 1.4). Prove N_{A4}(X) << X^{beta} for some beta<0.7784 (ideally beta=1/2+eps).

title: Lower the exponent 1/2 in Pasten's subexponential abc bound
credit: Extends H. Pasten, Invent. Math. 2024 (arXiv:2312.03566), Thm 1.4.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.01327 (2026 preprint): cited in refs; M does not depend on it.
plain: Unconditionally, abc is known only in very weak forms. Pasten (2024) proved that if a ≤ c^{1−η} then log c ≤ η^{-1} exp(κ√(log R · log log R)), with R = rad(abc). abc predicts log c ≤ (1+ε) log R + O(1). Replace the square root by any smaller power of log R.
math: For coprime $a+b=c$ with $R=\mathrm{rad}(abc)$, Pasten (Invent. Math. 2024, Thm 1.4) proves: if $a\le c^{1-\eta}$ then $\log c\le \eta^{-1}\exp\big(\kappa\sqrt{\log R\,\log_2 R}\big)$; and $\log c\le q\exp(\kappa\sqrt{\log R\log_2R})$ with $q=\min\{P(a),P(b),P(c)\}$. Prove either statement with $\exp((\log R)^{\theta})$ for some fixed $\theta<1/2$, or $\exp(O(\sqrt{\log R}))$.

title: One-level density of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions beyond support (−2,2)
credit: Özlük–Snyder (Canad. J. Math. 58, 2006; earlier 1999 work) and Rubinstein (Duke 2001) for support (−2,2); Katz–Sarnak (1999) density conjectures.
plain: Under GRH, the low-lying zeros of L(s,χ_d) for quadratic characters are known to follow the symplectic random-matrix law only for test functions whose Fourier transform is supported in (−2,2). Go beyond 2.
math: For the family of real primitive characters $\chi_{8d}$, $d$ odd squarefree, $X<d\le 2X$, and even Schwartz $\phi$ with $\operatorname{supp}\hat\phi\subset(-\sigma,\sigma)$, prove under GRH that $\frac1{|\mathcal F|}\sum_d\sum_{\gamma_d}\phi\!\big(\gamma_d\frac{\log X}{2\pi}\big)\to\int\phi(x)\big(1-\frac{\sin 2\pi x}{2\pi x}\big)dx$ for some $\sigma>2$.
lean_gap: Not formalized: needs sums over L-function zeros with multiplicity.

title: Push the GRH lower bound for Montgomery's F(alpha) beyond alpha = 1
credit: Goldston, Gonek, Özlük, Snyder (2000), 'On the pair correlation of zeros of the Riemann zeta-function', Proc. London Math. Soc.
plain: Montgomery's function F(α) is known only for |α|≤1 (on RH). Under GRH for Dirichlet L-functions, Goldston–Gonek–Özlük–Snyder proved F(α) ≥ 3/2−|α|−ε on 1≤|α|≤3/2, while the conjecture says F(α)=1 there. Improve this lower bound.
math: Assume GRH for all Dirichlet $L$-functions. Prove that for some $\delta>0$ and all $\alpha\in[1,1+\delta]$, $\liminf_{T\to\infty}F(\alpha,T)\ge \tfrac32-\alpha+\delta$, or prove $\liminf_T \int_{1}^{3/2}F(\alpha,T)\,d\alpha>1/8$ (the value forced by the GGOS bound).

title: Second moment of 3-torsion in imaginary quadratic class groups
credit: Cohen, Lenstra, 'Heuristics on class groups of number fields', LNM 1068 (1984); Davenport-Heilbronn (1971) for the first moment
plain: Davenport–Heilbronn showed the average of |Cl(K)[3]| over imaginary quadratic fields is 2, as Cohen–Lenstra predicts. Cohen–Lenstra also predict the average of |Cl(K)[3]|² is 6. Prove this, or at least that the average is bounded.
math: Let $K$ range over imaginary quadratic fields with $|D_K|<X$. Cohen–Lenstra ($\mathbb E\,\#\mathrm{Sur}(\mathrm{Cl}_K,H)=1$ for $H=(\mathbb Z/3)^2$) predict $\frac{1}{\#\{K\}}\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\to 6$. Prove this limit, or prove $\sum_K|\mathrm{Cl}_K[3]|^2\ll X$.

title: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
plain: Jörgens proved that a convex function on the whole plane whose Hessian determinant is 1 must be a quadratic polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent, u_xx·u_yy + u_xy², and ask whether the same rigidity holds for solutions on the elliptic branch.
math: Let $u\in C^4(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy $u_{xx}u_{yy}+u_{xy}^2=1$, $u_{xx}>0$ and $2u_{xy}^2<1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ (these are exactly the conditions for the linearized operator $u_{yy}\partial_{xx}+2u_{xy}\partial_{xy}+u_{xx}\partial_{yy}$ to be elliptic; they force $u$ convex with $0<\det D^2u=1-2u_{xy}^2\le1$). Prove or disprove that $u$ is a quadratic polynomial.

title: Critical NLS blow-up threshold on the cube surface
credit: Extension of Weinstein (Comm. Math. Phys. 1983) mass-critical threshold; related Strichartz work on flat cones by Ford and by Blair-Ford-Marzuola.
plain: In the plane, the focusing cubic Schrödinger equation needs at least the ground-state mass to blow up. On the surface of a cube, each corner is a cone with total angle 3π/2, which can hold a 'three-quarter' ground state. So the blow-up threshold should drop to three quarters of the planar one, and the claim is that it does exactly that.
math: Let $S$ be the surface of the unit cube with its flat metric, and let $\Delta$ be the Friedrichs extension of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\{\text{vertices}\})$. Let $Q$ be the ground state of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$, and put $m_*=\tfrac34\|Q\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^2)}^2$. For $iu_t+\Delta u+|u|^2u=0$ on $S$, prove: (i) every $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*$ gives a global $H^1$ solution; (ii) for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $u_0\in H^1(S)$ with $m_*<\|u_0\|_2^2<m_*+\varepsilon$ whose solution blows up in finite time. (Stronger, optional: blow-up data exist for every mass $m>m_*$; also decide whether there is blow-up at mass exactly $m_*$.)
lean_gap: Statement left as sorry by design.

title: Derivative loss in L4 Strichartz on the cube surface
credit: Blair, Ford, Marzuola, Strichartz estimates for the wave equation on flat cones / Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, arXiv:1003.0666.
results: s* >= 0 (trivial). No positive lower bound known. s* <= 1/4: Blair-Ford-Marzuola, Thm 1.5 (arXiv 1003.0666), loss 1/p for compact Euclidean surfaces with conical singularities, p=q=4; authors call the loss an artifact of the method.
plain: On the flat torus, the L4 space-time estimate for Schrodinger waves loses only epsilon derivatives (Bourgain). On the surface of a cube, which has eight cone points that diffract waves, only a loss of 1/4 derivative is known. Find the true loss: prove any loss below 1/4, or show some loss is necessary.
math: Let $S$ be the unit cube surface, $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension from $C_c^\infty(S\setminus\text{vertices})$, and $s^*=\inf\{s\ge0:\|e^{it\Delta}f\|_{L^4([0,1]\times S)}\le C_s\|f\|_{H^s(S)}\}$. Known: $0\le s^*\le\tfrac14$ (Blair–Ford–Marzuola). Prove $s^*<\tfrac14$, or $s^*>0$; ideally determine $s^*$ (conjecturally $0$).
lean_gap: Not formalized: needs Friedrichs Laplacian and Sobolev spaces on a cone surface.

title: Does an oscillating source lower the Strauss exponent?
results: Bound p_c<=1+sqrt2 is correct: John/Zhou iteration uses only |F(u)|<=C|u|^p and |F(u)-F(v)|<=C(|u|+|v|)^{p-1}|u-v|, both hold for g(t)|u|^p. The 'resonance predicts 2' heuristic (exp of int t^{1-p}) is arithmetically right but not an argument; a normal-form attempt (H''=g) just recycles the oscillating factor, so nothing is proved.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.28389 (2026 preprint): cited background on Strauss-type problems with time-dependent coefficients; the statement does not depend on it.
plain: For the 3D wave equation with source |u|^p, small smooth data give global solutions exactly when p > 1+√2 (Strauss). Multiply the source by a factor that oscillates periodically in time with average zero, such as cos t. The global-existence proof still works above 1+√2. Every blow-up proof below it breaks, because they all need the source to be positive. Is the true threshold strictly smaller?
math: Let $g$ be smooth, $2\pi$-periodic, $\int_0^{2\pi}g=0$, $g\not\equiv0$ (model $g=\cos t$). For $u_{tt}-\Delta u=g(t)|u|^p$ on $\mathbb R^{1+3}$ with data $\varepsilon(f,h)$, $f,h\in C_c^\infty$ (solutions in the usual weak/mild sense, e.g. $C([0,T);H^1)$ with John-type weighted bounds), let $p_c(g)=\inf\{p>1:\forall f,h\ \exists\varepsilon_0>0$ such that the solution is global for all $0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\}$. Since John/Zhou/Glassey global existence uses only $|g|u|^p|\lesssim|u|^p$ and the matching Lipschitz bound, $p_c(g)\le1+\sqrt2$. Is $p_c(g)<1+\sqrt2$? Determine $p_c(g)$ and whether it depends on $g$ (a heuristic predicts 2). For $1<p<p_c(g)$, determine the lifespan $T_\varepsilon$ as $\varepsilon\to0$ for suitable data.
lean_gap: Statement left as sorry by design.

credit: OpenAI, forced Navier–Stokes blow-up (Sep 2026, unrefereed PDF); Lions (1969) for α ≥ 5/4; Tao, averaged Navier–Stokes (arXiv:1402.0290).
