title: Heat with a cosine reaction
credit: H. Fujita 1966 (critical exponent); R. Pinsky 1997 (weighted Fujita problem, a >= 0)
plain: In u_t = u_xx + cos(x) u^2 the reaction term averages to zero over a period, but a second-order (homogenization) effect produces an effective +u^3 term, which in one dimension is exactly Fujita's borderline exponent where every positive solution of u_t = u_xx + u^3 blows up. Does every positive solution of the cosine equation blow up in finite time?
math: Let $d\ge1$, $a\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$ be $\mathbb Z^d$-periodic with $\int_{[0,1]^d}a=0$, $a\not\equiv0$. Consider $u_t=\Delta u+a(x)u^p$, $u(\cdot,0)=u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^d)$, $u_0\ge0$, $u_0\not\equiv0$. Prove: (i) if $1<p\le1+1/d$, every such solution blows up in finite time; (ii) if $p>1+1/d$, solutions with sufficiently small $u_0$ are global. Test case: $d=1$, $p=2$, $a=\cos(2\pi x)$ (equivalently $a=\cos x$ with $2\pi$-periodicity).

title: KdV with a cosine coefficient
plain: Put a cos x in front of the cubic term of the modified KdV equation on the circle. The energy and the mean are still conserved, but the L² norm is not, and the energy no longer has a definite sign. Can smooth solutions blow up in finite time?
math: Consider $u_t+u_{xxx}+(\cos(x)\,u^3)_x=0$ on $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z$ with real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)$. It is Hamiltonian, $u_t=\partial_x\frac{\delta H}{\delta u}$ with $H=\int(\tfrac12u_x^2-\tfrac14\cos(x)u^4)$, and conserves $\int u$ and $H$. However, $\frac{d}{dt}\int u^2=\frac12\int\sin(x)u^4$. Decide whether every such $u_0$ yields a global smooth solution, or whether $\|u(t)\|_{H^1}\to\infty$ in finite time for some $u_0$.

title: Liouville theorem for Lane-Emden with a shifted nonlinearity
plain: Gidas-Spruck: -Delta u = u^p has no positive solution on R^n for subcritical p. Replace u^p by the value of u^p at a shifted point x+e. Is there still no positive solution, for every subcritical p?
math: Let $n\ge3$, $1<p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$, $e\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Prove or disprove: there is no positive $u\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)$ with $-\Delta u(x)=u(x+e)^p$ for all $x$. (For $1<p<\frac n{n-2}$ the standard Mitidieri–Pohozaev test-function argument applies, since the shift is negligible at large scales; the open range is $\frac n{n-2}\le p<\frac{n+2}{n-2}$. One may also ask whether positive solutions exist for $p\ge\frac{n+2}{n-2}$.)

title: Mass-critical scattering on flat cones
credit: B. Dodson, global well-posedness and scattering for the defocusing L^2-critical NLS in d=2 (Duke Math. J. 2016)
results: Both trivial cases check out. For alpha=2pi/k, C_alpha=R^2/Z_k: the Friedrichs modes e^{ikmθ} with Bessel order k|m| match the Z_k-invariant plane functions, and Dodson applies for any mass, with mass scaled by k. For radial data the m=0 mode on the cone is the 2D radial Laplacian. The sign convention iu_t+Δu=+|u|^2u is defocusing.
plain: Dodson proved that the defocusing cubic Schrodinger equation in the plane scatters for every finite-mass initial state. Prove the same on every flat cone, a plane with a single conical singularity of total angle alpha. For alpha = 2pi/k it follows from Dodson by symmetry, and radial data are also easy. Every other angle, such as the surface of a cube corner (alpha = 3pi/2) or alpha > 2pi, is open.
math: For $\alpha>0$ let $\mathcal C_\alpha=(0,\infty)\times(\mathbb R/\alpha\mathbb Z)$ with metric $dr^2+r^2d\theta^2$ and $\Delta$ the Friedrichs extension of the Laplacian on $C_c^\infty(\mathcal C_\alpha)$. Prove that for every $\alpha>0$ and every $u_0\in L^2(\mathcal C_\alpha)$ the solution of $iu_t+\Delta u=|u|^2u$, $u(0)=u_0$, is global with $\|u\|_{L^4_{t,x}(\mathbb R\times\mathcal C_\alpha)}<\infty$, hence scatters in $L^2$. (Known: $\alpha=2\pi/k$, since $\mathcal C_{2\pi/k}=\mathbb R^2/\mathbb Z_k$ and Dodson applies to $\mathbb Z_k$-invariant data. Radial data for any $\alpha$, since the radial equation coincides with the 2D one.)
lean_gap: Not formalized: it needs the Friedrichs extension, Stone's theorem / the Schrodinger group on L^2 of the cone, mild L^2 solutions of NLS, and space-time Lebesgue norms.

title: Quintic Szego growth
credit: Gérard–Grellier (cubic Szegő equation, turbulent solutions); Thirouin, quadratic Szegő equation (arXiv:1710.01512).
plain: The cubic Szego equation on the circle is completely integrable, and Gerard-Grellier showed that its smooth solutions can have Sobolev norms that are unbounded in time. Decide whether the quintic Szego equation, which is presumably not integrable, also has smooth solutions with unbounded high Sobolev norms.
math: On $L^2_+(\mathbb T)=\{u\in L^2:\hat u(k)=0\ \forall k<0\}$ with Szego projector $\Pi$, consider $i\partial_tu=\Pi(|u|^4u)$, which is globally well posed in $H^s_+$, $s>1/2$, with conserved $\|u\|_{L^2}$, $(Du,u)$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}$. Decide whether there exist $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb T)\cap L^2_+$ and $s>1/2$ with $\limsup_{t\to\infty}\|u(t)\|_{H^s}=\infty$.
lean_gap: Not formalized: needs well-posedness theory for the quintic Szegő equation.

title: Ising spin at a cube corner
credit: Chelkak, Hongler, Izyurov, Conformal invariance of spin correlations in the planar Ising model, Ann. Math. 2015 (arXiv:1202.2838)
results: The CFT step is correct. With w=z^{4/3}, the apex spin has dimension (2pi/alpha)(1/8)=1/6, and 1/6+1/8=7/24. For alpha=2pi the formula gives back 1/4. The lattice description is right: the apex has degree 3 and axis vertices have degree 4. The beta_c value is right. The free-boundary infinite-volume limit exists by GKS monotonicity. The apex defect is irrelevant (energy dimension >0), so 7/24 should be universal.
plain: Glue three quarter-planes of the square grid into the surface of an infinite cube corner (a flat cone of angle 3π/2) and run the critical Ising model. Prove that the spin at the corner decorrelates with the exponent 7/24 predicted by conformal field theory.
math: Let $\Gamma$ be the union of the three quadrant lattices $\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2$ on the faces of $\partial\mathbb R_{\ge0}^3$, glued along the coordinate axes, with apex $o$ (degree 3; every other vertex has degree 4). Let $\langle\cdot\rangle$ be the infinite-volume limit of the nearest-neighbour Ising model at $\beta_c=\tfrac12\log(1+\sqrt2)$ with free boundary conditions on $\Gamma\cap\{\|x\|_\infty\le n\}$. Prove $\langle\sigma_o\sigma_x\rangle\asymp|x|^{-7/24}$ as $|x|\to\infty$.

title: Alternating quotients of knot groups
credit: Dunfield-Thurston, Finite covers of random 3-manifolds, Invent. Math. 2006 (arXiv:math/0502567), question on alternating quotients; Everitt / Liebeck-Shalev for Fuchsian groups
results: Computer-verified in a fresh script: trefoil (xyx=yxy) surjects onto A5 but not A6 or A7. Figure-eight (w=x^-1yxy^-1) surjects onto A4 and A6 but not A5, A7 or A8, and has no S3 quotient, as det=5 requires. n>=9 not rerun (would take more than 30s). The trefoil argument (centre maps trivially, factor through C2*C3, Miller's (2,3)-generation) is correct.
plain: The trefoil's group maps onto every alternating group A_n with n>=9, because modulo its centre it is the modular group. Show that every nontrivial knot group maps onto A_n for all large n, or at least for infinitely many n, and bound the last exception in terms of the knot.
math: Let $K\subset S^3$ be a nontrivial knot and $G_K=\pi_1(S^3\setminus K)$. (a) Prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for all $n\ge N(K)$, and bound $N(K)$ in terms of the crossing number. (b) Weaker: prove that $G_K$ surjects onto $A_n$ for infinitely many $n$, or even for one $n\ge5$. Data (exhaustive search over pairs of conjugate even permutations, meridians $x,y$ with $wx=yw$): for the trefoil ($w=xy$) a surjection exists exactly for $n=5$ and $n\ge9$, since every surjection kills the centre and factors through $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\cong C_2*C_3$, and Miller proved $(2,3)$-generation of $A_n$ for $n\ne3,6,7,8$. For the figure-eight knot ($w=x^{-1}yxy^{-1}$) a surjection exists for $n=6,9,10$ and not for $n=5,7,8$. Is $N(4_1)=9$, i.e. does $G_{4_1}$ surject onto $A_n$ for every $n\ge9$?

title: Infinitely many knot types in the symmetric ABC flow
credit: Etnyre & Ghrist (2000), arXiv:math-ph/9906021; Enciso, Peralta-Salas (and Romaniega), arXiv:2006.15033.
premise_risks: arXiv:2609.17449 (Szumiński–Llibre, 2026 preprint): cited only as related perturbative work; nothing in the statement depends on it.
plain: Steady Euler flows can carry knotted streamlines, and generic high-frequency Beltrami fields on the torus contain every knot. Show that the most-studied explicit example, the ABC flow with A = B = C = 1, has closed streamlines tied in infinitely many different knots.
math: Let $X=(\sin z+\cos y,\ \sin x+\cos z,\ \sin y+\cos x)$ on $\mathbb T^3=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ (a curl eigenfield, $\nabla\times X=X$). Prove that the periodic orbits of $X$ that lie in some embedded 3-ball $B\subset\mathbb T^3$ realize infinitely many distinct knot types (as knots in $B\cong$ a ball in $\mathbb R^3$). Stronger: every knot type is realized.

title: Knotted billiards in a regular tetrahedron
credit: Extends Jones–Przytycki (Lissajous knots and billiard knots, 1998) and Koseleff–Pecker, 'Every knot is a billiard knot', arXiv:1106.5600; periodic orbits in polyhedra: Bedaride–Rao arXiv:1104.1051.
plain: A billiard ball bouncing periodically inside a regular tetrahedron, without hitting edges or corners, traces a closed polygon in space. Is any such polygon knotted, and do infinitely many different knot types occur?
math: Call a periodic billiard trajectory in a regular tetrahedron $T\subset\mathbb R^3$ admissible if it never meets an edge or vertex of $T$ and its image is an embedded closed polygon. (a) Does some admissible trajectory form a nontrivial knot? (b) Prove that the set of knot types of admissible periodic trajectories is infinite.

title: Galois groups of Keller fibers
plain: Gallagher (2026) built, for every n>=3, a polynomial map C^3->C^3 with constant nonzero Jacobian whose general fibre has exactly n points. Determine the symmetry (monodromy/Galois) group of how those n points are permuted.
math: Let $H_n:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ be Gallagher's Keller map of geometric degree $n$ (A. Gallagher, \emph{An infinite family of counterexamples to the Jacobian Conjecture in dimension three}, Zenodo 2026, doi:10.5281/zenodo.21479195), so $[\mathbb C(x,y,z):H_n^*\mathbb C(X,Y,Z)]=n$. For each $n\ge3$ determine the Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x,y,z)/H_n^*\mathbb C(X,Y,Z)$ (equivalently the monodromy group of the $n$-sheeted covering over a general point), as a permutation group of degree $n$; and the arithmetic group over $\mathbb Q$.

title: Keller maps injective on integer points
plain: Take a polynomial map of 3-space with integer coefficients whose Jacobian determinant is identically 1 (a Keller map). Show that if it never sends two different integer points to the same point, then it is a polynomial automorphism.
math: Let $F\in\mathbb{Z}[x,y,z]^3$ with $\det JF\equiv 1$. Prove that if $F|_{\mathbb{Z}^3}$ is injective, then $F$ has a polynomial inverse (equivalently, by Bia{\l}ynicki-Birula--Rosenlicht, $F$ is injective on $\mathbb{C}^3$).

title: Keller monodromy is everything
plain: Since 2026 there are polynomial maps of 3-space with constant nonzero Jacobian that are not invertible (counterexamples to the Jacobian conjecture), and every number n >= 3 of points in a generic fibre occurs. Show that for every n the fibre points can be permuted in every possible way by going around loops, i.e. the monodromy group can be the full symmetric group S_n.
math: Prove that for every $n\ge3$ there is a polynomial map $F:\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^3$ with $\det JF\in\mathbb C^{\times}$, of geometric degree $[\mathbb C(x):\mathbb C(F)]=n$, whose geometric monodromy group (the Galois group of the Galois closure of $\mathbb C(x_1,x_2,x_3)/\mathbb C(F_1,F_2,F_3)$, acting on the $n$ generic fibre points) is $S_n$.

title: Closed-form Euler blow-up
plain: Smooth compactly supported starting data for the 3D Euler equations that blow up in finite time are now known to exist, but the construction is an infinite iterative series. Give such data as an explicit formula.
math: Find an explicit divergence-free $u_0=\nabla\times\big(P(x)e^{-|x|^2}\big)$ with $P\in\mathbb{Q}[x_1,x_2,x_3]^3$ (or another explicitly specified finite closed-form class) such that the unforced 3D incompressible Euler solution on $\mathbb{R}^3$ with $u(0)=u_0$ has finite maximal smooth lifespan.

title: Drum tones of superellipses
plain: Take the region |x|^p + |y|^p <= r^p, scaled to have area 1. At p = 2 it is a disk, which has the lowest possible bass note of any region of that area (Faber–Krahn). As p grows to infinity it becomes a square, whose note is higher. Show that the note rises steadily the whole way from p = 2 to infinity.
math: For $p\in[2,\infty)$ let $D_p=\{(x,y):|x|^p+|y|^p\le r_p^p\}$ with $r_p$ chosen so that $|D_p|=1$, and let $\lambda_1(p)$ be the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of $-\Delta$ on $D_p$. Prove that $\lambda_1$ is strictly increasing on $[2,\infty)$, with $\lambda_1(2)=\pi j_{0,1}^2$ and $\lambda_1(p)\uparrow2\pi^2$ as $p\to\infty$.

title: Multiplicities on the Fermat quartic
plain: The surface x^4+y^4+z^4 = 1 has exactly the 48 symmetries of a cube. Show its Laplace eigenvalues repeat no more often than those symmetries force (at most 3 times), except possibly for finitely many eigenvalues.
math: Let $S=\{x^4+y^4+z^4=1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the induced metric (isometry group the hyperoctahedral group of order 48, whose irreducible representations have dimension $\le3$). Prove that all but finitely many eigenvalues of $\Delta_S$ have multiplicity $\le3$.
review_note: F

title: Frozen vortices for Kuramoto on a cube
plain: Identical Kuramoto oscillators sit on the grid of a cube's surface. Besides full synchrony, there is a 'longitude' state with a vortex at the centre of the top face and an antivortex at the centre of the bottom face. Prove that this state is a linearly stable equilibrium for every grid size.
math: Let $Q_n$ be the vertex–edge graph of the $n\times n$ subdivided surface of the cube, and $\dot\theta_i=\sum_{j\sim i}\sin(\theta_j-\theta_i)$. Prove that for every odd $n\ge3$ there is an equilibrium $\theta^*$ with the cube's 4-fold rotational symmetry about the vertical axis and winding number $\pm1$ around the central plaquettes of the top and bottom faces, whose Jacobian (the Laplacian with edge weights $\cos(\theta^*_j-\theta^*_i)$) has kernel exactly $\mathrm{span}(\mathbf 1)$ and is otherwise positive. (More generally: for which $n$ does $Q_n$ have a stable non-synchronous equilibrium?)

review_note: T

title: Non-flat free-boundary minimal disks in the superball
plain: In a round ball the only free-boundary minimal disks are flat slices through the centre (Nitsche). The superball x^4+y^4+z^4 <= 1 has nine flat ones, cut by its mirror planes. Is there also one that is not flat? A natural candidate has threefold symmetry about the diagonal (1,1,1).
math: For $p>2$ let $B_p=\{|x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p\le1\}$. Decide whether $B_4$ (more generally $B_p$) contains an embedded minimal disk $\Sigma$ with $\partial\Sigma\subset\partial B_p$, meeting $\partial B_p$ orthogonally, that is not contained in a plane. Specifically, show that there is one invariant under the rotation by $2\pi/3$ about the axis $\mathbb R(1,1,1)$ and under $v\mapsto-v$.
review_note: W

title: Rotation-proof lattice-point-poor shapes
plain: Among convex shapes of area A, how few lattice points can a shape be guaranteed to contain under every rotation about the origin? Can any shape do much better than a disc centred at the origin?
math: For $A>0$ let $m(A)=\inf\{\sup_{\theta}\#(\rho_\theta K\cap\mathbb Z^2): K\subset\mathbb R^2\text{ compact convex},\ |K|=A\}$. Decide whether $m(A)\ge A-O_\varepsilon(A^{1/4+\varepsilon})$.
review_note: T

title: Rupert superballs
plain: A cube can pass through a hole drilled in a copy of itself; a round ball cannot. Show that every superball between them, |x|^p+|y|^p+|z|^p ≤ 1 with p > 2, can.
math: Let $B_p=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:|x_1|^p+|x_2|^p+|x_3|^p\le1\}$ and $q=p/(p-1)$. Prove that for every $p\in(2,\infty)$ there are orthogonal projections $\pi_1,\pi_2$ of $\mathbb R^3$ onto planes and a rigid motion $\rho$ with $\rho(\pi_1(B_p))\subset\operatorname{int}\pi_2(B_p)$. By central symmetry this is equivalent to: there are orthonormal pairs $(a_1,a_2),(b_1,b_2)$ in $\mathbb R^3$ with $\|\cos t\,b_1+\sin t\,b_2\|_q>\|\cos t\,a_1+\sin t\,a_2\|_q$ for all $t$.
review_note: N

title: Prime Markov triples
plain: Markov triples are positive integer solutions of x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz. Are there infinitely many in which all three numbers are prime?
math: Decide whether infinitely many solutions $(x,y,z)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^3$ of $x^2+y^2+z^2=3xyz$ have $x,y,z$ all prime.
review_note: W

title: Burgers with degenerate critical dissipation
plain: Critical half-Laplacian dissipation keeps Burgers smooth. Let that dissipation switch off quadratically at one point of the circle. Do shocks form there?
math: Let $a(x)=1-\cos x$ and consider $u_t+uu_x+\Lambda^{1/2}\big(a\,\Lambda^{1/2}u\big)=0$ on $\mathbb{T}$, $\Lambda=(-\partial_x^2)^{1/2}$. Decide whether every real $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{T})$ yields a global smooth solution.
review_note: L

title: Minimal-mass blow-up with reflection
plain: Consider the 2D Schrödinger equation in which the self-interaction at each point uses the density at the mirror point -x. Below the ground-state mass, solutions exist forever. Show that the only solutions that blow up with exactly the ground-state mass are the explicit pseudo-conformal ground-state solutions centred at the origin.
math: Let $Q>0$ be the radial solution of $\Delta Q-Q+Q^3=0$ on $\mathbb R^2$. Consider $iu_t+\Delta u+|u(-x,t)|^2u=0$ with $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb R^2)$ and $\|u_0\|_{L^2}=\|Q\|_{L^2}$. Prove that if $u$ blows up at a finite time $T$, then there are $\theta\in\mathbb R$ and $\lambda>0$ with $u(t,x)=e^{i\theta}\frac{\lambda}{T-t}\,Q\!\Big(\frac{\lambda x}{T-t}\Big)\exp\!\Big(i\frac{\lambda^2}{T-t}-i\frac{|x|^2}{4(T-t)}\Big)$.
review_note: T

title: Riesz-transform Schrodinger equation
plain: Couple a 2D Schrodinger wave to the Riesz transform of its own density. Mass is conserved, but there is no energy. Do smooth solutions live forever?
math: Consider $iu_t+\Delta u=u\,R_1(|u|^2)$ on $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^2$, $\widehat{R_1f}(\xi)=-i\frac{\xi_1}{|\xi|}\hat f(\xi)$. Decide whether every $u_0\in H^1(\mathbb{R}^2)$ gives a global solution in $C(\mathbb{R},H^1)$.
review_note: C

title: Shifted Fujita equation
plain: In the plane, every positive solution of u_t = Delta u + u^2 blows up (u^2 is exactly Fujita-critical in dimension 2). Does this survive when u^2 is replaced by the product of the values of u one unit to the left and one unit to the right?
math: Let $e=(1,0)$. Prove or disprove: for every $0\le u_0\in C_c(\mathbb R^2)$ with $u_0\not\equiv0$, the solution of $u_t=\Delta u+u(x-e,t)\,u(x+e,t)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ blows up in finite time.
review_note: L

title: Unforced blow-up near the forced one
plain: The 2026 forced Navier–Stokes blow-up uses a force that is smooth through the blow-up time. Can the force be made to vanish identically at the blow-up instant while staying smooth up to and including that instant?
math: Do there exist $T>0$ and $f\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3\times(0,\infty))$ with $f(\cdot,T)\equiv0$ such that the 3D Navier–Stokes solution on $\mathbb R^3$ with $u_0=0$ and force $f$ satisfies $\limsup_{t\uparrow T}\|u(t)\|_{L^\infty}=\infty$? (Requiring $f\equiv0$ on $[T-\delta,T]$ for some $\delta>0$ instead would be equivalent to unforced blow-up from smooth data, which is the Millennium problem.)
review_note: A

title: Random Wang tiles
plain: (Corrected.) Draw n Wang tiles whose four edge colours are chosen uniformly at random from c colours, and let c grow with n ≈ λc². How likely is the set to tile the plane? Show the probability has a limit F(λ) and find the critical λ above which tiling is almost certain.
math: Let $T_1,\dots,T_n$ be i.i.d. Wang tiles, each with its four edge colours i.i.d. uniform in $[c]$ and no rotations allowed. Let $n=\lfloor\lambda c^2\rfloor$ and $c\to\infty$. Prove that $F(\lambda)=\lim_{c\to\infty}\Pr(\{T_i\}\text{ tiles }\mathbb Z^2)$ exists for every $\lambda>0$. Determine $\lambda_c=\inf\{\lambda:F(\lambda)=1\}$; a first-moment heuristic suggests $\lambda_c=1$. Also determine $F$ on $(0,\lambda_c)$.
review_note: A

title: Period-doubling torus bundles
plain: Build a once-punctured torus bundle by reading the period-doubling word as a product of the two basic shear matrices. Show its hyperbolic volume per letter settles to a limit as the word grows.
math: Let $W_n\in\{a,b\}^{2^n}$ be the length-$2^n$ prefix of the fixed point of $a\mapsto ab,\ b\mapsto aa$ ($n\ge1$). Let $\phi_n\in SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ be the product obtained from $W_n$ via $a\mapsto R=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $b\mapsto L=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, and let $M_n$ be the once-punctured torus bundle with monodromy $\phi_n$ (hyperbolic since $W_n$ contains both letters). Prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(M_n)/2^n$ exists.
review_note: L

title: Thue–Morse Lorenz knots
plain: Turn the first 2^n letters of the Thue–Morse word into a periodic orbit of the Lorenz flow, and so into a knot K_n. For n >= 4 these knots appear to be hyperbolic. Their volume grows only in proportion to n, the logarithm of the word length, not in proportion to the length itself. Prove that, and find the constant.
math: Let $K_n$ be the Lorenz knot with Lorenz word $t_0t_1\cdots t_{2^n-1}$ (the length-$2^n$ Thue–Morse prefix, $0\mapsto x$, $1\mapsto y$; this word is primitive, since Thue–Morse is overlap-free and $t_{[0,2^n)}=w\bar w$). Prove that $S^3\setminus K_n$ is hyperbolic for all $n\ge4$ and that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathrm{vol}(S^3\setminus K_n)/n$ exists and is positive. Determine the limit.
review_note: T

title: Is R(3,10) equal to 40 or 41?
credit: Radziszowski dynamic survey 'Small Ramsey Numbers'; Angeltveit (2023/2025).
premise_risks: Angeltveit's upper bound is computer-assisted; if it had an error the range would revert to 40-42
An unpublished construction or nonexistence proof could exist
plain: The Ramsey number R(3,10) is the fewest people at a party that guarantees either 3 mutual acquaintances or 10 mutual strangers. It is known to be 40 or 41, and nobody knows which. Settle it: either build a 40-vertex triangle-free graph with no 10 pairwise non-adjacent vertices, or show none exists.
math: Let $R(3,10)$ be the least $n$ such that every graph on $n$ vertices contains $K_3$ or an independent set of size $10$. Known: $40\le R(3,10)\le 41$. Decide whether there exists a triangle-free graph $G$ on $40$ vertices with $\alpha(G)\le 9$ (equivalently whether $R(3,10)=41$).
review_note: Known: Lower bound 40: Exoo (1989), a (3,10)-graph on 39 vertices. Upper bound 41: V. Angeltveit, 'R(3,10) <= 41', arXiv:2401.00392, Electron. J. Combin. 32(4) (2025) P4.30, improving 42 (Goedgebeur-Radziszowski 2013). Pandey-Ravi, arXiv:2601.03572 (Jan 2026), study structural properties of hypothetical critical graphs, quoting the older range 40-42 and assuming R(3,10)=42; they do not settle the value. No 2025-2026 resolution found.

title: Four-colour triangle Ramsey number R(3,3,3,3)
credit: Radziszowski survey; Chung (1973); Fettes-Kramer-Radziszowski (2004); Tatarevic (2026 preprint).
premise_risks: The bound 60 is an unrefereed 2026 preprint resting on unverified SAT runs; the safe published bound is 62
Problem may be stated with whichever upper bound the board accepts
plain: Colour every edge of a complete graph with one of four colours. How many vertices force a single-coloured triangle? The answer is known to lie between 51 and 60 (the 60 coming from a 2026 computer-assisted preprint). Narrow or close this gap.
math: Let $R_4(3)=R(3,3,3,3)$ be the least $n$ such that every 4-edge-colouring of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic triangle. Known: $51\le R_4(3)\le 62$ (refereed), and $\le 60$ in a 2026 computer-assisted preprint. Improve either bound, i.e. exhibit a 4-colouring of $K_{51}$ with no monochromatic triangle, or lower the upper bound (below 60, or confirm 60 rigorously). Ultimately determine $R_4(3)$; it is conjectured to be $51$.
review_note: Known: Lower 51: F. Chung (1973). Upper 62: Fettes-Kramer-Radziszowski, Ars Combin. 72 (2004). Upper 60: M. Tatarevic, arXiv:2610.36648 (2026 preprint). It reduces to 296,081 SAT instances (UNSAT by Kissat and CaDiCaL); the reductions are in Lean/Mathlib, but the SAT exclusions are taken as a premise; extensive AI assistance is disclosed. Boza, arXiv:2603.10851 (2026), improves other multicolour bounds and cites 62 for R_4(3).

title: Does the Steiner system S(2,6,51) exist?
credit: Handbook of Combinatorial Designs (Abel-Greig table); Banakh-Hetman-Ravsky (2025).
premise_risks: Exact open list taken from arXiv:2511.05191 as summarised; 51 being open should be double-checked against Abel's latest tables
Exhaustive search may be far harder than v=46 so the problem could be practically intractable
plain: Can you choose 6-element groups from 51 objects so that every pair of objects lies together in exactly one group (that would take 85 groups)? The arithmetic allows it, but no one has built one or proved it impossible. This is the smallest such undecided case for groups of size 6.
math: Decide whether there is a family $\mathcal B$ of $6$-subsets of a $51$-set $V$ such that every $2$-subset of $V$ lies in exactly one member of $\mathcal B$ (a $2$-$(51,6,1)$ design; necessarily $|\mathcal B|=85$ and each point is in $10$ blocks).
review_note: Known: Necessary conditions v ≡ 1, 6 (mod 15). The Handbook of Combinatorial Designs (Abel-Greig) listed 29 undecided v. Banakh-Hetman-Ravsky, arXiv:2511.05191 (2025), construct S(2,6,226) and S(2,6,441), leaving 27 open: 51, 61, 81, 166, 231, 256, 261, 286, 316, 321, 346, 351, 376, 406, 411, 436, 471, 501, 561, 591, 616, 646, 651, 676, 771, 796, 801. S(2,6,46) does not exist (Houghten-Thiel-Janssen-Lam, 2001, exhaustive computation).

title: Ramsey multiplicity constant of K_4
credit: Erdos; Thomason; Parczyk-Pokutta-Spiegel-Szabo (2022/2024); Grzesik-Lee-Lidicky-Volec.
premise_risks: Asymptotic constant; Lean formalization would need the limit definition, and 'improve a bound' is not a yes/no claim
plain: In any red/blue colouring of the edges of a huge complete graph, some fraction of all 4-vertex sets must be single-coloured (all 6 edges the same colour). The minimum possible fraction is known only to lie between about 0.0296 and 0.03015. Pin it down further, or find its exact value.
math: Let $c_4=\lim_{n\to\infty}\min_{G,|V(G)|=n}\big(k_4(G)+k_4(\bar G)\big)/\binom n4$. Known: $0.0296<c_4\le U=4551721\cdot 2^{-24}\cdot 3^{-2}<0.030145$ (Parczyk–Pokutta–Spiegel–Szabó). Formal target: improve the upper bound strictly, i.e. prove $c_4<4551721\cdot 2^{-24}\cdot 3^{-2}$ (more generally improve either bound or determine $c_4$).
review_note: Known: Upper: Thomason (1989) < 1/33; Parczyk-Pokutta-Spiegel-Szabo, arXiv:2206.04036, Found. Comput. Math. (2024): c_4 <= 4551721·2^{-24}·3^{-2} < 0.030145 (blow-ups of a 768-vertex Cayley graph). Lower: Niess (arXiv:1207.4714) 0.0287; Sperfeld; Grzesik-Lee-Lidicky-Volec: c_4 > 0.0296 (cited in PPSS). Erdos's conjecture c_4 = 1/32 was refuted by Thomason.

title: Total colouring of planar graphs with maximum degree 6
credit: Behzad/Vizing Total Colouring Conjecture; planar-case literature (Sanders-Zhao, Wang, Roussel, Zhu).
premise_risks: Zhu's 2026 maximal-planar result is unrefereed
Infinite family; formalization needs planarity in Mathlib, which is limited
plain: A total colouring colours both vertices and edges so that touching objects (adjacent vertices, edges sharing an end, an edge and its endpoint) get different colours. It is conjectured that Δ+2 colours always suffice, where Δ is the maximum degree. For planar graphs this is proved for every Δ except Δ=6: show every planar graph with maximum degree 6 has a total colouring with 8 colours.
math: Prove that every simple planar graph $G$ with $\Delta(G)=6$ satisfies $\chi''(G)\le 8$ (or find a counterexample).
review_note: Known: Delta <= 5: Kostochka (all graphs). Planar Delta=7: Sanders-Zhao. Planar Delta >= 8: earlier results (Borodin et al.). Planar Delta=6 is known under extra hypotheses: no 4-cycles (Wang et al.), no adjacent triangles (Sun et al.), each vertex misses some k-cycle with 3<=k<=8 (Roussel), no 4-fan (Zhu-Xu), and special 4-cycle conditions (arXiv:2609.19503, 2026); see arXiv:2507.12737. E. Zhu, arXiv:2610.32717 (2026 preprint): every maximal planar graph with Delta <= 6 is totally 8-colourable; this does not cover all planar graphs because completing to a triangulation can raise Delta.

title: Largest cap set in F_3^7
credit: Edel; Potechin; Thackeray (2022).
premise_risks: Thackeray's no-289 result is an arXiv paper with computer-assisted counting; refereed status unclear
Large gap; exact value may be out of reach
plain: A cap set is a set of points in the 7-dimensional grid {0,1,2}^7 (arithmetic mod 3) containing no three points on a line. The biggest known one has 236 points, and it is known that 289 points is impossible. Find a bigger cap or prove a better upper bound.
math: Let $r_3(7)$ be the maximum size of $A\subseteq\mathbb F_3^7$ containing no three distinct points $x,y,z$ with $x+y+z=0$ (equivalently, no three collinear points). Known: $236\le r_3(7)\le 288$. Improve either bound; in particular, is there a cap of size $237$? Ultimately determine $r_3(7)$.
review_note: Known: Lower 236: Edel et al. construction (Edel's cap tables), matched but not beaten by FunSearch (Romera-Paredes et al., Nature 2023) and X-evolve (arXiv:2508.07932, best known 236 in dimension 7, 512 in dimension 8). Upper 288: Thackeray, 'The cap set problem: up to dimension 7', arXiv:2206.09804, Theorem 4.2 (no 289-cap 7-flat, hence no larger cap). Exact values known through dimension 6 (r_3(6)=112, Potechin 2008).

title: Strong edge colouring with maximum degree 4: 20 or 21 colours?
credit: Erdos-Nesetril conjecture; Cranston; Huang-Santana-Yu.
premise_risks: A 2026 improvement to 20 might exist that the searches missed
plain: A strong edge colouring gives edges colours so that any two edges that touch, or are joined by a third edge, get different colours. Erdős and Nešetřil conjectured that graphs with maximum degree 4 need at most 20 colours; it is proved that 21 suffice. Close the one-colour gap.
math: Prove that every graph $G$ with $\Delta(G)\le4$ has strong chromatic index $\chi'_s(G)\le20$ (Erdos-Nesetril bound $\tfrac54\Delta^2$), or find a graph with $\Delta\le4$ and $\chi'_s=21$.
review_note: Known: chi'_s <= 22: Cranston (2006, arXiv:math/0601623). chi'_s <= 21: Huang-Santana-Yu, Electron. J. Combin. 25(3) (2018) P3.31 (arXiv:1806.07012). Lower bound 20 is attained by the blow-up of C_5 (each vertex replaced by 2 vertices). Related: packing edge-colouring results for Delta <= 4 (Involve 18(2), 2025) do not give 20. Delta=3 is settled (10; Andersen, Horak-He-Trotter).

title: Oriented chromatic number of planar graphs (18 vs 80)
credit: Courcelle; Raspaud-Sopena; Marshall; Sopena surveys.
premise_risks: The precise sharper statement ('improve to 79') is incremental; the real interest is a substantially better bound
plain: Orient every edge of a planar graph. An oriented colouring colours vertices so adjacent vertices differ and all arcs between two colour classes point the same way. Every oriented planar graph can be coloured with 80 colours, and some need 18. The gap has barely moved since 1994: narrow it.
math: Let $\chi_o(\mathcal P)=\max\chi_o(\vec G)$ over orientations of simple planar graphs ($\chi_o$ = least order of a tournament receiving a homomorphism). Known $18\le\chi_o(\mathcal P)\le80$. Formal target: strict improvement of the upper bound, $\chi_o(\mathcal P)\le79$ (the lower-bound direction, an example with $\chi_o\ge19$, is the alternative improvement and is not the formal Claim).
review_note: Known: Upper 80: Raspaud-Sopena, Inform. Process. Lett. 51 (1994), via acyclic 5-colourability (Borodin). Lower bound history: 15 (Sopena), 16 and 17 (Marshall), 18 (Marshall, Ars Combin. 2015). Clow, 'MAD phase transitions in the oriented chromatic number', arXiv:2607.22915 (2026), confirms both bounds are still current.

title: Order of magnitude of ex(n, C_8)
credit: Erdos; Bondy-Simonovits; Furedi-Simonovits survey.
premise_risks: Famous long-standing problem; may be judged better suited to the main set or too hard
plain: How many edges can a graph on n vertices have without containing a cycle of length 8? It is known to be at most about n^{5/4}, but the best constructions are smaller by a polynomial factor, unlike lengths 4, 6 and 10 where matching constructions exist. Find a C_8-free graph with about n^{5/4} edges, or prove a smaller upper bound.
math: Determine whether $\mathrm{ex}(n,C_8)=\Theta(n^{5/4})$. Known: $\Omega(n^{6/5})\le\mathrm{ex}(n,C_8)\le O(n^{5/4})$. (In general $\mathrm{ex}(n,C_{2k})=O(n^{1+1/k})$ by Bondy-Simonovits, with matching order known only for $k\in\{2,3,5\}$; the lower bound $n^{6/5}$ comes from generalized hexagons and equals the Lazebnik-Ustimenko-Woldar bound $n^{1+2/(3k-3+\epsilon)}$ with $k=4,\epsilon=1$.) Equivalently (given the upper bound): are there $c>0$ and $N$ such that for every $n\ge N$ some $C_8$-free graph on $n$ vertices has $\ge c\,n^{5/4}$ edges? Any exponent above $6/5$ would also be progress.
review_note: Known: Upper O(n^{5/4}): Bondy-Simonovits (1974); constants improved by Verstraete, Pikhurko, Bukh-Jiang. Lower Omega(n^{6/5}): incidence graph of a generalized hexagon (girth 12), matching Lazebnik-Ustimenko-Woldar n^{1+2/(3k-3+ε)} at k=4, ε=1; see Furedi-Simonovits, arXiv:1306.5167. Order known only for C_4, C_6, C_10 (Benson, Wenger, generalized polygons). 2026 work on C_8 (arXiv:2607.03856 generalized Turán; arXiv:2607.16103 planar Turán) does not touch the ordinary exponent.

title: An effective bound for the sum-free excess
credit: Bedert (2025) remark; Eberhard-Green-Manners (2014).
premise_risks: EGM's argument might yield a very weak explicit rate on careful bookkeeping; the (log N)^{-c} target avoids this but may be much harder
Truth could be N/3 + N^{1-c} or much smaller; no conjecture on the true rate
plain: Every set of N nonzero integers contains a sum-free subset (no x+y=z inside it) of size a bit more than N/3; Bedert (2025) showed the excess grows at least like log log N. It is also known that you cannot always beat N/3 by more than o(N), but that proof gives no rate. Prove a quantitative version: some N-element sets have no sum-free subset larger than N/3 + N/(log N)^c.
math: Let $S(N)=\min_{A\subset\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\},\,|A|=N}\max\{|B|:B\subseteq A\text{ sum-free}\}$. Known: $N/3+c\log\log N\le S(N)\le N/3+o(N)$, with the $o(N)$ ineffective. Prove that there is $c>0$ with $S(N)\le N/3+O\big(N/(\log N)^{c}\big)$. Any explicitly quantified $o(N)$ (e.g. $N/(\log\log N)^{c}$) would be partial progress.
review_note: Known: Lower: Erdos (1965) $N/3$; Alon-Kleitman $(N+1)/3$; Bourgain $(N+2)/3$; Bedert, arXiv:2502.08624 (2025) $N/3+c\log\log N$. Upper: Eberhard-Green-Manners, Annals 180 (2014), arXiv:1301.4579: $N/3+o(N)$, ineffective.

title: Covering systems with a large minimum modulus
credit: Erdős (minimum modulus problem); Hough; Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba; Owens (42); Dai–Li–Li–Yi (14000)
premise_risks: 14000 bound is a Nov 2026 preprint, not yet refereed; refereed bound is 616,000
a construction with minimum modulus > 42 might exist unpublished
plain: A covering system is a finite list of arithmetic progressions a_i mod m_i, all with different moduli, such that every integer lies in at least one of them. Erdős asked whether the smallest modulus can be made as large as you like; Hough proved it cannot. The largest smallest modulus anyone has actually achieved is 42, while the best proof only shows it is at most 14,000. Find a covering with smallest modulus at least 43, or prove a much smaller upper bound.
math: Let $M^*$ be the largest integer $M$ for which there exist $k\ge1$, distinct integers $M\le m_1<\dots<m_k$ and residues $a_i$ with $\bigcup_i (a_i+m_i\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$. Known: $42\le M^*<14000$ (and $\le 13278$ by a further computer-assisted calculation, same preprint). Decide whether $M^*\ge 43$, and more generally narrow the gap (e.g. prove $M^*\le 1000$).
review_note: Known: Lower 42: Owens, 'A covering system with minimum modulus 42' (BYU thesis 2014); still the record per the survey arXiv:2208.09720 and the constructions table in arXiv:2611.15110. Upper bounds: Hough 10^16 (Annals 2015); Balister-Bollobas-Morris-Sahasrabudhe-Tiba 616,000 (2022); Dai-Li-Li-Yi, 'On the moduli of distinct covering systems', arXiv:2611.15110 (Nov 2026 preprint): < 14000 (13278 with extra computation). Squarefree moduli: Cummings-Filaseta-Trifonov <= 118 (arXiv:2211.08548), lowered to <= 7 by Dai-Li-Li-Yi.

title: Two sixth powers equal to four
credit: Lander–Parkin–Selfridge (1967); Ekl; Resta–Meyrignac
premise_risks: MathWorld's 'no 6.2.4 known' is unattributed and may lag distributed searches (EulerNet, Wróblewski's tables)
no refereed search limit specific to 6.2.4 located
plain: Can the sum of two sixth powers of positive integers equal the sum of four sixth powers? For sixth powers, three-equals-three examples are plentiful and two-equals-five examples are known, but nobody has found a two-equals-four example or proved there are none.
math: Does $x_1^6+x_2^6=y_1^6+y_2^6+y_3^6+y_4^6$ have a solution in positive integers? (Any such solution is automatically nontrivial: cancelling a common term would leave a $6.1.3$ solution, itself unknown.) This is a boundary case $m+n=k$ of the Lander–Parkin–Selfridge conjecture for $k=6$, where only $6.3.3$ solutions are known.
review_note: Known: MathWorld, 'Diophantine Equation--6th Powers': 'No solutions are known to the 6.2.3 or 6.2.4 equations'; 'No 6.1.n solutions are known for n<=6' (Lander–Parkin–Selfridge 1967; Guy, UPINT); Ekl (1996/1998) found no 6.2.2 solutions with sums below about $7.25\times10^{26}$. Smallest 6.2.5 solutions: Resta & Meyrignac, Math. Comp. 72 (2003). Parametric 6.3.3 solutions are classical (e.g. Brudno, Math. Comp. 1976). No refereed search bound specific to 6.2.4 found.

title: Integer complexity of powers of two
credit: D. Rawsthorne; R. K. Guy; H. Altman; J. Zelinsky
premise_risks: He's 2^126 verification is in an arXiv appendix (unrefereed computation)
may require a qualitatively new idea; known defect theory handles only finitely many k
plain: The complexity of a positive integer n is the fewest 1's needed to write n using only +, × and parentheses. Writing 2^k as (1+1)(1+1)...(1+1) uses 2k ones. Is that always optimal? It has been checked by computer for every 2^k up to 2^126, but no proof is known.
math: Let $\|n\|$ be the least number of $1$'s in an expression for $n$ built from $1$, $+$, $\times$ and parentheses. Prove or disprove: $\|2^k\|=2k$ for all $k\ge1$ (more strongly, $\|2^k3^\ell\|=2k+3\ell$ for $(k,\ell)\ne(0,0)$).
review_note: Known: Verified $\|2^k3^\ell\|=2k+3\ell$ for $k\le48$ and all $\ell$: Altman, 'Integer complexity: algorithms and computational results', Integers 18 (2018), arXiv:1606.03635 (earlier $k\le21$, Altman–Zelinsky arXiv:1207.4841). Pure powers of 2: no counterexample for $2^k\le 2^{126}\approx10^{38}$, and $\|2^i3^j5^k\|=2i+3j+5k$ checked for $2^i3^j5^k\le10^{36}$, $k\le5$ (Q. He, 'Improved algorithms for integer complexity', arXiv:2308.10301). Question attributed to Rawsthorne (in Guy, UPINT F26). Konyagin–Oganesyan arXiv:2603.20876 (2026): average-case estimates, not this question.

title: How many groups of order 2048?
credit: Besche–Eick–O'Brien; Eick–O'Brien; Conway–Dietrich–O'Brien
premise_risks: mainly a large computation; exact value may need counting-without-listing techniques rather than new theory
the 1.78e15 target encodes an expert expectation (first three digits), not a proved heuristic
g(2^10) value: check the corrected OEIS figure before publishing
plain: The number of groups is known exactly for every order below 2048; order 1024 alone has about 49 billion. For order 2048 = 2^11 the exact number of groups is still unknown, and only a lower bound of about 1.774 × 10^15 is proved. Determine the number, or at least prove that it is below 1.78 × 10^15, as experts expect.
math: Let $g(n)$ be the number of isomorphism classes of groups of order $n$. Determine $g(2^{11})$. Known: $g(2^{11})\ge 1\,774\,274\,116\,992\,170$, the number of groups of order $2^{11}$ of $2$-class $2$ (exponent-$2$ Frattini quotient class 2). Natural intermediate target: prove $g(2^{11})<1.78\times10^{15}$, i.e. that the class-2 groups determine the first three significant digits.
review_note: Known: $g(n)$ known for all $n<2048$ (Besche–Eick–O'Brien, 'The groups of order at most 2000', ERA-AMS 2001, plus later orders); $g(2^{10})=49\,487\,365\,422$ (later corrected to $49\,487\,367\,289$ in OEIS A000001). Lower bound $g(2^{11})\ge1\,774\,274\,116\,992\,170$ (Eick–O'Brien, 'Enumerating p-groups', J. Austral. Math. Soc. 1999; quoted in Conway–Dietrich–O'Brien, Math. Intelligencer 2008). No explicit nontrivial upper bound specific to $2^{11}$ located; general Higman–Sims bounds are far off.

title: Squeezing the square-lattice site percolation threshold
credit: van den Berg–Ermakov (1996); Wierman (1995); Wierman–Oberly (2024)
premise_risks: an unreviewed lower bound 0.5567 already exists online; if it is confirmed, the lower-bound target moves
the Wierman–Oberly abstract mentions 'a series of recent improvements', so an intermediate upper bound may also exist
the 2024 upper bound is in conference proceedings rather than a journal
plain: Colour each square of an infinite chessboard black independently with probability p. There is a critical p above which an infinite connected black cluster appears; simulations put it at about 0.5927, but nobody has a formula. The best proved statements only say it lies between 0.556 and 0.6669. Prove a tighter bound on either side.
math: Let $p_c=p_c^{\mathrm{site}}(\mathbb Z^2)$. Known rigorously $0.556<p_c<0.666894$. Formal target: improve the upper bound at its published precision, $p_c<0.6668$ (more generally improve either endpoint rigorously).
review_note: Known: Lower $p_c>0.556$: van den Berg & Ermakov, Random Structures Algorithms 8 (1996) 199–212. Unreviewed claim $p_c\ge0.5567$ (computer-assisted, personal page kaust-a-laut.github.io, not peer reviewed). Upper $p_c<0.666894$: Wierman & Oberly, 'A new upper bound for the site percolation threshold of the square lattice', in Combinatorics, Graph Theory and Computing (Springer, 2024), improving Wierman's 0.679492 (CPC 1995, substitution method). Numerical $p_c\approx0.59274605$ (Jacobsen 2015 and others; non-rigorous).

title: Densest packing of regular heptagons
credit: Kuperberg & Kuperberg (1990); Kallus (2013); after Hales–Kusner (2016)
premise_risks: global optimality could appear in a recent preprint not found
likely a large computer-assisted project (difficulty may be underestimated)
plain: Copies of a regular heptagon (any rotations and positions allowed) are placed in the plane without overlapping. The best known arrangement uses rows of heptagons pointing alternately up and down and covers about 89.27% of the plane. Prove no arrangement does better.
math: Let $\delta(P_7)$ be the maximal packing density of congruent copies of the regular heptagon $P_7$ in $\mathbb R^2$ (isometries allowed). Prove $\delta(P_7)=\frac{2}{97}\left(-111+492\cos\frac{\pi}{7}-356\cos^2\frac{\pi}{7}\right)\approx 0.892691$, the density of the best double-lattice packing.
review_note: Known: Best double-lattice density: Kuperberg & Kuperberg, DCG 5 (1990); value as stated (AMS Visual Insight, Baez 2014). Pentagon optimum = double lattice: Hales & Kusner, arXiv:1602.07220 (computer-assisted). Kallus, 'Pessimal packing shapes', Geom. Topol. (arXiv:1305.0289): heptagon is a local pessimum for double-lattice density. Local optimality of double lattices: Kallus–Marcus arXiv:1509.02241. The heptagon is believed to be the worst-packing convex shape, unproved. No proof of global optimality.

title: No three in line: beat 3n/2
credit: Dudeney (1917); Hall–Jackson–Sudbery–Wild (1975); Guy–Kelly (1968)
premise_risks: the problem is famous (Dudeney); only the constant improvement is asked, not the 2n question
Epoch AI hosts a closely related target (1.8n, arbitrarily large n), so a solution may surface there first
plain: How many points of an n-by-n grid can you pick so that no three of them lie on one straight line (at any angle)? Each row holds at most two, so 2n is the ceiling, and explicit constructions from 1975 give about 1.5n for large n. Find, for all large n, a construction with at least cn points for some constant c > 1.5.
math: Let $f(n)$ be the largest size of $S\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}^2$ with no three collinear points. Known: $(\tfrac32-o(1))n\le f(n)\le 2n$. Prove there is $c>3/2$ with $f(n)\ge cn$ for all sufficiently large $n$.
review_note: Known: Lower $(3/2-o(1))n$: Hall, Jackson, Sudbery, Wild, JCTA 18 (1975). Upper $2n$ (pigeonhole); Guy–Kelly (1968) heuristic $f(n)\sim(\pi/\sqrt3)n\approx1.814n$. $f(n)=2n$ attained computationally for all $n\le46$ and some larger even $n$ (Flammenkamp); Epoch AI's page reports tightness for $n\le70$. For $k\ge3$, the no-$(k+1)$-in-line maximum is $kn$ for large $n$: arXiv:2607.05255 (July 2026), after arXiv:2502.00176 and arXiv:2510.17743; arXiv:2508.07632's randomised constructions are vacuous at $k=2$. Epoch AI lists 'more than 1.8n for arbitrarily large n' as an open problem.

title: Kissing number in five dimensions: at most 43
credit: Mittelmann–Vallentin (2010); Bachoc–Vallentin (2008)
premise_risks: a recent k-point SDP computation might already give 43 or lower without wide notice
the 3-point SDP value is ≈44.998, so 43 needs a genuinely stronger relaxation or structural input
plain: How many unit balls can touch a central unit ball in 5-dimensional space without overlapping? A configuration with 40 has been known since 1873, and the best proved upper limit, from large semidefinite computations, is 44 (the computed bound is about 44.998). Prove that 44 is impossible.
math: Let $\tau_5$ be the maximum size of a set $X\subset S^4$ with $\langle x,y\rangle\le 1/2$ for all distinct $x,y\in X$. Known $40\le\tau_5\le44$. Prove $\tau_5\le 43$.
review_note: Known: Lower 40: $D_5$ root system (Korkine–Zolotareff 1873); non-isometric 40-configurations by Leech (1967) and Cohn–Rajagopal (arXiv:2412.00937). Upper: Coxeter 48; Odlyzko–Sloane 46.345 (1979); 45 Bachoc–Vallentin (2008); 44 Mittelmann & Vallentin, Experiment. Math. 19 (2010), arXiv:0902.1105 (SDP value ≈44.998). New SDP upper bounds in dimensions 11–23 (de Laat, Leijenhorst et al.) do not touch $n=5$.

title: A macroscopic upper bound for tetrahedron packing
credit: Gravel–Elser–Kallus (2011); Chen–Engel–Glotzer (2010); Hilbert's 18th problem
premise_risks: the 0.99 benchmark is illustrative; the real question is any macroscopic bound
an unpublished SDP computation for tetrahedra could exist
plain: Regular tetrahedra cannot fill space, and the best packings found fill about 85.6% of it. Yet the best proved limit only says a packing fills at most 1 − 0.00000000000000000000000026 of space. Prove a macroscopic upper bound, for instance that no packing of congruent regular tetrahedra fills more than 99% of space.
math: Let $\delta_T$ be the maximal packing density of congruent regular tetrahedra in $\mathbb R^3$. Known $0.856347\le\delta_T\le1-2.6\times10^{-25}$. Formal target: the macroscopic bound $\delta_T\le0.99$.
review_note: Known: Lower $4000/4671$: Chen, Engel, Glotzer, DCG 43 (2010), arXiv:1001.0586 (dimer packings; cf. Kallus–Elser–Gravel, Torquato–Jiao). Upper $1-2.6\times10^{-25}$: Gravel, Elser, Kallus, 'Upper bound on the packing density of regular tetrahedra and octahedra', DCG 46 (2011), arXiv:1008.2830. SDP framework for congruent copies: Dostert, Guzmán, de Oliveira Filho, Vallentin, arXiv:1308.4893 (computed for pentagons, not tetrahedra). Translative case: arXiv:1208.0420.

title: Does the trefoil have a symbiont?
credit: Brittenham & Hermiller, arXiv 2601.18757 (2026), Cor. 4.2 and Sec. 3/5
premise_risks: Fast-moving area: a late-2026 preprint could settle u(10_6)
Mirror conventions: the bound u(3_1#10_6) ≤ 3 is for a specific mirror pairing
u(10_6)=2 would not settle the trefoil question, since another partner could exist
plain: The unknotting number of a knot is the fewest crossing changes needed to turn it into an unknotted loop. In 2025 it was shown that tying two knots together end to end can need fewer changes than the two knots need separately, and in 2026 that every torus knot except possibly the trefoil has a partner like this. Does the trefoil, the simplest knot, also have such a partner? The most likely candidate is the 10-crossing knot 10_6, whose own unknotting number is still unknown (it is 2 or 3).
math: Write $u(K)$ for the unknotting number and $\#$ for connected sum. Knots $K,K'$ are symbionts if $u(K\#K')<u(K)+u(K')$. Is there a knot $K$, with some choice of mirror image, such that $u(3_1\#K)<1+u(K)$? By Scharlemann's theorem any such $K$ has $u(K)\ge2$. Concrete subquestion: is $u(10_6)=3$? Brittenham–Hermiller prove $u(3_1\#10_6)\le3$ for the mirror choice with $|\sigma(3_1\#10_6)|=2$, so $u(10_6)=3$ would give a positive answer.
review_note: Known: Additivity fails: $u(7_1\#\overline{7_1})\le5$ (Brittenham–Hermiller, arXiv:2506.24088, 2025). Every non-trivial torus knot except possibly $T(2,3)$ has a symbiont (Cor. 4.2), and $u(3_1\#10_6)\le3$ with $u(10_6)\in\{2,3\}$ (Thm 1.3); the paper calls deciding $u(10_6)$ an interesting open problem (Brittenham–Hermiller, arXiv:2601.18757, 2026). Scharlemann: $u(K\#K')\ge2$ for non-trivial $K,K'$. arXiv:2608.25256 (2026) obtains 194 new unknotting numbers of alternating knots with d-invariants and Owens' theorem; it began as an attempt to prove $u(10_6)=3$ and says $u(10_6)$ is still unknown. Lee (arXiv:2609.09861, 2026) also lists $10_6$ as unresolved in $[2,3]$.

title: Equilateral stick number versus stick number
credit: Rawdon & Scharein (2002); restated as open in Cantarella–Rechnitzer–Schumacher–Shonkwiler, arXiv 2508.18263
premise_risks: A strict gap needs exact lower bounds on s_eq, so the problem may be out of reach in practice
Exact s(K) is unknown for many ≤10-crossing knots; 'agree' means only that the best known bounds coincide
plain: Build a knot out of straight sticks joined end to end. The stick number of a knot is the fewest sticks that can make it. If all the sticks must also be the same length, you might need more. Is there any knot that really does need more sticks when they all have to be the same length?
math: For a knot type $K$ let $s(K)$ be the minimum number of edges of a polygonal knot of type $K$, and $s_{eq}(K)$ the minimum over equilateral polygons. Formal Claim: there is a knot type $K$ with $s_{eq}(K)>s(K)$ (¬Claim: $s_{eq}=s$ for all $K$; the infinite-family variant is not formalized).
review_note: Known: Posed by Rawdon–Scharein (2002). After the equilateral 9-stick $9_{29}$ (Theorem 4, proved via a Millett–Rawdon perturbation condition), no knot with ≤10 crossings has differing best known bounds for $s$ and $s_{eq}$ (Cantarella–Rechnitzer–Schumacher–Shonkwiler, arXiv:2508.18263, Sec. 4). Lower bounds for $s$ (Calvo's crossing-number bound, superbridge index) do not depend on edge lengths. Upper bounds on $s_{eq}$ in terms of crossing number: Kim–No–Oh, arXiv:1401.7383.

title: Ropelength lower bound for the trefoil
credit: Denne–Diao–Sullivan (2006) bound; ropelength problem of Cantarella–Kusner–Sullivan and Buck–Simon
premise_risks: The Schoen preprint is unrefereed and has several Zenodo versions; its claimed bound could be wrong, or have been raised in a newer version
Normalization: diameter convention (15.66 = 31.32 in radius convention)
16.372 is numerical, not a certified upper bound
plain: Tie a knot in a rope of thickness 1 using as little rope as possible. For the simplest knot, the trefoil, computer experiments find tight knots using about 16.37 units of rope. The last refereed proof shows that every knotted rope needs at least 15.66 units, and a 2026 computer-assisted preprint claims 15.76. Raise the proven lower bound for the trefoil substantially, ideally to 16.
math: For a $C^{1,1}$ closed curve, $\mathrm{Rop}=\mathrm{length}/(2\,\mathrm{reach})$; $R(3_1)=\inf$ over trefoils (attained). Known $15.66\le R(3_1)\lesssim16.372$ (refereed lower bound; numerical value), with an unrefereed 2026 computer-assisted claim $R(K)>15.7561$ for all nontrivial $K$. Formal target: $R(3_1)\ge16$.
review_note: Known: Lower: $\mathrm{Rop}\ge15.66$ for every nontrivial knot (Denne–Diao–Sullivan, Geom. Topol. 10 (2006), arXiv:math/0408026), improving 12 (Cantarella–Kusner–Sullivan). Unrefereed: $\mathrm{Rop}(K)>15.75608926$ for every nontrivial $K$ via interval-arithmetic certificates (A. A. Schoen, 'Endpoint Tangents and a New Universal Lower Bound for the Ropelength of Nontrivial Knots', Zenodo, Sep 2026, v5.0.0, not peer reviewed). Klotz, arXiv:2611.14234 (Nov 2026), lists 31.51217852 (radius-normalized, so 15.756 diameter-normalized) for crossing number 3–8 as the current best, citing Schoen. Upper: numerical tight trefoil below 16.372 (DDS abstract). Minimizers exist (Cantarella–Kusner–Sullivan 2002; Gonzalez–Maddocks–Schuricht–von der Mosel 2002).

title: Does Antihydra halt?
credit: bbchallenge community (Antihydra found 2024; reformulation by mxdys et al.); Ligocki, 'BB(6) is Hard (Antihydra)'
premise_risks: The TM ⇔ arithmetic equivalence rests on bbchallenge wiki and its formal proofs, not a refereed paper. M is self-contained either way.
Collatz-like; likely far beyond current methods
plain: Start with 8 and repeatedly multiply by 3/2, rounding down. Keep score: +2 for every even number you see and −1 for every odd number. Does the score ever go negative? This is exactly the question of whether a specific 6-state Turing machine, called Antihydra, ever halts. Answering it is the first obstacle to determining the sixth Busy Beaver number.
math: Let $a_0=8$ and $a_{n+1}=\lfloor 3a_n/2\rfloor$. For $n\ge1$ let $E_n=\#\{i<n:a_i\text{ even}\}$ and $O_n=\#\{i<n:a_i\text{ odd}\}$. Does there exist $n$ with $O_n>2E_n$? Equivalently (bbchallenge), does the 6-state 2-symbol Turing machine 1RB1RA_0LC1LE_1LD1LC_1LA0LB_1LF1RE_---0RA halt from a blank tape? The conjecture is that it never halts.
review_note: Known: Simulated to $2^{38}$ rule steps without halting (bbchallenge wiki). Under a random-walk heuristic (steps +2/−1), the chance of ever reaching −1 from the current score is about $10^{-2.87\times10^{10}}$ (wiki). It is listed as an undecided 'probviously non-halting' cryptid on the BB(6) wiki page; the current BB(6) champion exceeds $10\uparrow\uparrow10\uparrow\uparrow10\uparrow\uparrow8$ (mxdys, June 2025). BB(5) is determined (arXiv:2509.12337). Related: Mahler's 3/2 problem; Dubickas on integer sequences from linear maps. More BB(6) cryptids, all unresolved: arXiv:2610.22603 (2026).

title: Translational tiling of the plane with two tiles: decidable?
credit: Yang & Zhang, arXiv 2506.19295 (open problem stated); Abel et al., arXiv 2509.07906 (Table 3)
premise_risks: Fast-moving area (k went 5→4→3 in 2025, and the 3D monotile in 2026); a late-2026 preprint could settle k=2
Connected vs. possibly-disconnected tiles may differ; the main statement allows arbitrary finite tiles
plain: You are given two shapes made of grid squares, and you may only slide copies of them around, never rotate them. Can copies of the two shapes cover the whole infinite grid with no gaps or overlaps? With one shape there is an algorithm that always answers this. With three shapes, one of them in several pieces, it was proved in 2025 that no algorithm can exist. Two shapes is the open case.
math: Given finite $F_1,F_2\subset\mathbb Z^2$, decide whether there exist $A_1,A_2\subseteq\mathbb Z^2$ with $(F_1+A_1)\sqcup(F_2+A_2)=\mathbb Z^2$, i.e. every point of $\mathbb Z^2$ lies in exactly one translate $F_j+a$, $a\in A_j$. Is this problem decidable? (Variant: also require $F_1,F_2$ to be connected polyominoes.)
review_note: Known: k=1: decidable (Beauquier–Nivat 1991 for polyominoes; Bhattacharya 2020, periodic tiling conjecture in $\mathbb Z^2$, for arbitrary finite $F$). k=3: co-RE-complete with three polyominoes, one disconnected and two connected of constant size; two trominoes suffice for a periodic subset of 2D (Abel, Akitaya, Chung, Demaine et al., 'Undecidability of Tiling with a Tromino', arXiv:2509.07906, 2025; Table 3 lists 2D/2 pieces/translation as OPEN). k=4, possibly disconnected: Yang–Zhang, arXiv:2506.19295 (2025), who list the two-tile case as open. k=5 connected: Kim, arXiv:2508.10067. Two tiles in $\mathbb Z^2\times G_0$: undecidable (Greenfeld–Tao, arXiv:2108.07902). With rotations, two tiles: undecidable (arXiv:2506.11628). A single polycube in 3D, translations only: undecidable (arXiv:2610.12392, Oct 2026).

title: A polyomino of odd order
credit: Golomb / Klarner rectifiable-polyomino program; Stewart & Wormstein (1992); Reid
premise_risks: Reflections allowed (Golomb's convention); a rotations-only version could differ
Reid's rectifiable-polyomino page (not loaded) might list an odd-order example. OEIS says none is known.
plain: Some shapes made of squares, like the L-tetromino, can tile a rectangle. The order of such a shape is the fewest copies that can do it. Apart from rectangles themselves (order 1), every shape with a known order needs an even number of copies, and order 3 is proved impossible. Is there a non-rectangular polyomino whose order is odd?
math: For a polyomino $P$ that tiles some rectangle with congruent copies (rotations and reflections allowed), let $\mathrm{ord}(P)$ be the minimum number of copies in such a tiling. Does there exist a non-rectangular $P$ with $\mathrm{ord}(P)$ odd? First test case: $\mathrm{ord}(P)=5$.
review_note: Known: Order 3 is impossible: Stewart & Wormstein, 'Polyominoes of order 3 do not exist', JCTA 61 (1992) 130–136. Maltby, 'Trisecting a rectangle', JCTA 66 (1994): no non-rectangular 3-piece congruent dissection; M. Reid noted on math-fun that the 5-, 7- and 9-piece dissection cases remain open. Odd tilings, as opposed to odd minimal tilings, exist: Reid, 'Many L-shaped polyominoes have odd rectangular packings', Ann. Comb. 18 (2014) 341–357. OEIS A126140 (maximum order for n cells): 'No example of a non-rectangular polyomino is known for which its order is odd.'

title: Is Grundy's game eventually periodic?
credit: Berlekamp, Conway & Guy, Winning Ways; computations by A. Flammenkamp
premise_risks: Computed range: '239' and '235' are superscript-lost renderings (2^39 and 2^35 most likely); not verified from a clean source
Classic problem with no clear modern angle
plain: In Grundy's game, players take turns splitting a pile of coins into two smaller piles of different sizes, and whoever cannot move loses. The game's theory reduces to one number per pile size, its Grundy value. These values have been computed for piles of hundreds of billions of coins and show no repeating pattern yet, though Berlekamp, Conway and Guy conjectured that they eventually repeat. Do they?
math: Let $g(0)=g(1)=g(2)=0$ and for $n\ge3$ let $g(n)=\operatorname{mex}\{g(a)\oplus g(b): a+b=n,\ 1\le a<b\}$, where $\oplus$ is bitwise XOR. Is $g$ eventually periodic, i.e. are there $N,p\ge1$ with $g(n+p)=g(n)$ for all $n\ge N$? (Weaker open question: is $g$ bounded?)
review_note: Known: Berlekamp–Conway–Guy (Winning Ways) conjecture eventual periodicity; Wikipedia says it is unresolved. Flammenkamp's octal-games page, Table 2 entry for Grundy's game: values computed for all n up to '239', most likely $2^{39}$ with the superscript lost. The largest known value is 297, attained at n = 21544358589, and 1287 rare values are known, the largest at 48399022. Wikipedia's text reads 'first 235 values', most likely $2^{35}$. OEIS A002188. Golomb's periodicity for finite subtraction games does not apply.

title: Odd plus odd is even
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: The sum of two odd natural numbers is even.
math: For all $a,b\in\mathbb N$, if $a$ and $b$ are odd then $a+b$ is even.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 2 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: n² + n is even
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: For every integer n, the number n² + n is even.
math: For all $n\in\mathbb Z$, $2\mid n^2+n$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 4 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Sum of the first n odd numbers
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Adding up the first n odd numbers 1 + 3 + 5 + … gives n².
math: For all $n$, $\sum_{i<n}(2i+1)=n^2$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 8 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Nicomachus: sum of cubes
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: The sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the sum of the first n numbers.
math: For all $n$, $\sum_{i=0}^{n} i^3=\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n} i\right)^2$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 16 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Coins of 3 and 5
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Every whole number from 8 upward can be paid exactly with coins worth 3 and 5.
math: For every $n\ge 8$ there are $a,b\in\mathbb N$ with $n=3a+5b$.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 32 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Party of six (R(3,3) ≤ 6)
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Among any six people, some three all know each other or some three are all strangers.
math: Every simple graph on 6 vertices contains a triangle or an independent set of size 3.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 64 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Erdős–Szekeres monotone subsequences
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: Any list of rs + 1 distinct real numbers has an increasing run of r + 1 of them or a decreasing run of s + 1 of them (not necessarily consecutive).
math: For $f:\{0,\dots,rs\}\to\mathbb R$ injective there is a set of $r+1$ indices on which $f$ is strictly increasing, or a set of $s+1$ indices on which it is strictly decreasing.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 128 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.

title: Dilworth's theorem
credit: classical result with known proof
plain: In any finite partially ordered set, the largest number of pairwise incomparable elements equals the smallest number of chains needed to cover everything.
math: For every finite poset $P$ there are $k$, an antichain of size $k$, and a partition of $P$ into $k$ chains.
review_note: Submission test. Estimated proof length about 256 lines; using Mathlib lemmas is allowed. Test problems do not count toward the leaderboards.
